Hapag-Lloyd will revise its Inland Fuel Floater for applicable inland transportation services in Italy. The carrier attributed the adjustment to continued volatility in international energy markets and fluctuations in diesel prices. The new rates will apply from 2 November 2026 for shipments not subject to Federal Maritime Commission regulations. For FMC-regulated shipments, the revised levels will take effect on 21 November 2026. Revised Italy inland fuel rates Transport mode Current rate New rate Truck transport 16% 15% Combined rail and truck 7.5% 10% Rail only 0% 7% The adjustment covers Fuel Origin Inland and Fuel Destination Inland charges for import and export inland haulage to and from Italy. The revised Inland Fuel Floater applies to all container types. Tariff date criteria For import shipments, Hapag-Lloyd will determine the applicable tariff according to the date the container is collected from the port. For FMC-regulated exports, the tariff date will be based on the full container’s gate-in date at the original port. For non-FMC exports, the applicable tariff will be determined by the vessel’s departure date. articles.title: Bureau Veritas grants type approval to WinGD’s variable compression technology
articles.summary: Bureau Veritas Marine & Offshore has granted Type Approval to WinGD’s Variable Compression Ratio (VCR) technology, marking an important step in the development of more efficient marine dual-fuel engines. The technology allows marine engines to adjust their compression ratio according to o perating conditions and fuel...
articles.body: Bureau Veritas Marine & Offshore has granted Type Approval to WinGD’s Variable Compression Ratio (VCR) technology, marking an important step in the development of more efficient marine dual-fuel engines. The technology allows marine engines to adjust their compression ratio according to o perating conditions and fuel selection. This helps optimize combustion, improve fuel efficiency and reduce emissions. Unlike conventional marine engines, which operate with a fixed compression ratio, WinGD’s system enables adjustments during operation. Improving marine engine efficiency WinGD’s VCR technology works by changing the piston position to adjust the volume of the combustion chamber. This allows the engine to operate with a compression ratio suited to its current requirements. The system is designed to improve the performance of WinGD’s X-DF dual-fuel engines across different operating conditions. It also offers efficiency benefits during part-load operation, when vessels operate at reduced engine loads. According to Bureau Veritas, the technology can support lower fuel consumption and greenhouse gas emissions by optimizing engine performance. The system’s mechanical configuration does not change the engine’s footprint or installation requirements. This could support its integration into newbuild vessels and potential future retrofit projects. Type approval supports technology development The approval represents an important milestone for WinGD as the marine industry seeks technologies that improve operational efficiency while supporting the transition to lower-carbon fuels. “WinGD’s Variable Compression Ratio (VCR) technology represents a major breakthrough in marine engine innovation,” said Dominik Schneiter, Chief Executive Officer of WinGD. Schneiter added that the technology enables the company’s X-DF engines to improve fuel efficiency and performance by adjusting compression ratios according to engine load. Christophe Chauviere, Marine & Offshore Technical & Operations Excellence Senior Vice-President at Bureau Veritas, said the technology allows engine performance to be optimized across different fuels and operating conditions. The approval comes as shipowners and operators increasingly focus on fuel flexibility, operational efficiency and compliance with evolving environmental requirements. While the technology has received Type Approval, the announcement does not identify specific vessel installations or provide quantified fuel savings.

articles.summary: Kuehne+Nagel reported strong financial results for the third quarter of 2026, with higher revenue and earnings across all four business units. articles.body: Kuehne+Nagel reported strong financial results for the third quarter of 2026, with higher revenue and earnings across all four business units. The logistics group recorded net turnover of CHF 7.4 billion, up 22% compared with the same period last year. Operating profit (EBIT) increased by 53% to CHF 435 million, while net earnings rose by 53% to CHF 316 million. The improvement was supported by higher freight volumes, increased gross profit and stronger operational efficiency. Following its nine-month performance, Kuehne+Nagel raised its full-year 2026 recurring EBIT guidance to CHF 1.5–1.6 billion. Sea Logistics returns to volume growth Kuehne+Nagel’s Sea Logistics division reported net turnover of CHF 2.7 billion in the third quarter, an increase of 20% year-on-year. EBIT rose by 55% to CHF 172 million, while the conversion rate reached 32%. Sea freight volumes increased by 5% during the quarter, marking a return to growth. The company attributed the improvement mainly to market share gains on Asia outbound and transatlantic trade lanes. Growth was also supported by the expansion of its China-origin controlled freight business. By the end of September 2026, cumulative Sea Logistics volumes had reached 3.3 million TEU. Air Logistics delivers strong performance Air Logistics continued to grow, with net turnover increasing by 38% to CHF 2.4 billion. The division’s EBIT climbed 84% to CHF 169 million, supported by higher demand for transport services linked to cloud infrastructure and semiconductor customers. Air freight volume growth accelerated to 10% in the third quarter, compared with 3% in the previous quarter. Cumulative volumes reached 1.7 million tonnes by the end of September. Meanwhile, Road Logistics reported a 40% increase in EBIT to CHF 28 million, while Contract Logistics recorded EBIT growth of 7% to CHF 66 million. Full-year earnings outlook raised Kuehne+Nagel said its third-quarter performance reflected growth across its logistics operations. “Kuehne+Nagel delivered strong third-quarter 2026 results, reflecting the resilience of our operations and validating our strategy of profitable growth,” said Stefan Paul, CEO of Kuehne+Nagel International AG. The company also highlighted a new long-term partnership with Amazon and AWS as part of its strategy to support future growth. Based on its performance during the first nine months of 2026, Kuehne+Nagel now expects recurring EBIT of CHF 1.5–1.6 billion for the full year.

articles.title: Sea-Intelligence: IMF Outlook: Container Shipping Under Strain
articles.summary: In issue 787 of the Sea-Intelligence Sunday Spotlight, we analysed the IMF October 2026 WEO report, from a container shipping perspective. The report predicts that world trade volume growth will drop from 5.0% in 2025 to 4.7% in 2027. In advanced economies, import demand is projected to be 5.0% in 2026 but soften to...
articles.body: In issue 787 of the Sea-Intelligence Sunday Spotlight, we analysed the IMF October 2026 WEO report, from a container shipping perspective. The report predicts that world trade volume growth will drop from 5.0% in 2025 to 4.7% in 2027. In advanced economies, import demand is projected to be 5.0% in 2026 but soften to 4.2% in 2027. This means that demand is not growing fast enough to absorb all the newly built vessel capacity entering service. Source: Sea-Intelligence.com, Sunday Spotlight, issue 787 Direct bilateral trade between the US and China has also contracted because of the trade war. As shown in Figure 1, after new tariffs were put in place in 2025, Chinese exports sent directly to the US fell by ‑22% over 12 months. During that same period, US exports to China dropped by ‑25%. However, overall trade volumes did not collapse, because the production went to other places. Chinese producers redirected 52% of their products to other Asian countries, and US exporters redirected 17%. Instead of shipping directly from China to the US, manufacturers are now sending parts to countries like Vietnam, Malaysia, and Indonesia. The products are put together there and then shipped to the US. This keeps trade volumes steady, but for the manufacturers and shippers, this makes logistics much more complicated, adds extra stops at ports, and increases costs. At the same time, an artificial intelligence (AI) boom is impacting trade. Trade in AI hardware has reached record highs compared to global GDP. While the money spent on AI trade has grown a lot, the actual physical weight of these goods has barely grown. This shows that the boom is driven by high prices rather than large physical volumes. While the physical microprocessors are normally moved by air, the heavy materials needed to build AI data centres are moved in ocean containers, providing important heavy cargo for shipping lines.

articles.title: Dual-fuel fleet passes 500 ships on the water as investment exceeds $200 billion
articles.summary: More than 500 dual-fuel container ships and vehicle carriers are now operating worldwide, with total investment in dual-fuel ships delivered and on order surpassing $200 billion USD, according to the latest World Shipping Council (WSC) Dual-Fuel Fleet Dashboard. As of September 2026, 503 dual-fuel ships were on the...
articles.body: Dual-fuel fleet passes 500 ships on the water as investment exceeds $200 billion in International Shipping News , Shipping: Emission Possible 23/10/2026 More than 500 dual-fuel container ships and vehicle carriers are now operating worldwide, with total investment in dual-fuel ships delivered and on order surpassing $200 billion USD, according to the latest World Shipping Council (WSC) Dual-Fuel Fleet Dashboard. As of September 2026, 503 dual-fuel ships were on the water, up 41% from 358 at the same time last year. A further 849 ships are on order, bringing the total delivered or on order to 1,352 ships. These ships are designed to operate on either conventional marine fuels or alternative fuel types, including renewable and lower-emission fuels, helping prepare the fleet for the transition to cleaner shipping. “The container ship and vehicle carrier industry have committed more than $200 billion to ships that can run on cleaner fuels, with more than 500 already sailing and hundreds more on the way,” said Joe Kramek, President & CEO of the World Shipping Council. “The investment is happening, but these ships need commercially competitive alternative fuels to deliver their full potential to reduce emissions.” The latest figures show that alternative-fuel-capable ships remain the dominant choice for container ship and vehicle carrier orders. By deadweight tonnage, they account for 65% of container ship orders and 97% of vehicle carrier orders, compared with 23% across the rest of the global shipping fleet. However, as the overall orderbook has expanded, orders for conventional-fuelled ships have also increased compared with a year ago. This comes amid continued uncertainty over global greenhouse gas regulation at the International Maritime Organization (IMO), highlighting the importance of clear global rules to support future investment decisions. “Ships ordered today will be operating for decades. Shipping companies and fuel producers need certainty to make the investments that will shape the future fleet and its fuel supply,” Joe Kramek said. WSC strongly supports a global greenhouse gas measure through the IMO, in line with its 2023 GHG Strategy. A global measure is essential to closing the cost gap between conventional and renewable and near-zero emission fuels, while providing clear, consistent rules for international shipping. Without a global framework, shipping also risks facing a growing patchwork of regional emissions regulations, adding complexity and cost to global trade. “We need a global measure with clear rules and strong, consistent enforcement that gives companies the confidence to invest in the production of cleaner fuels and the infrastructure needed to supply them,” Joe Kramek said. “We trust IMO member states can come together to deliver that framework. Every delay means increased uncertainty, making the transition harder and costlier for the global economy.” The updated WSC Dual-Fuel Fleet Dashboard is available at: https://www.worldshipping.org/dual-fuel-fleet-dashboard Source: World Shipping Council 2026-10-23 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.title: Product Tankers: Less Cargo, Higher Earnings
articles.summary: A market paradox seems to be forming in the product tanker market. In its latest weekly report, shipbroker Xclusiv said that “the product tanker market has experienced an extraordinary freight rally between early August and mid-October 2026, despite a significant contraction in global refined petroleum product trade....
articles.body: Product Tankers: Less Cargo, Higher Earnings in Hellenic Shipping News 23/10/2026 A market paradox seems to be forming in the product tanker market. In its latest weekly report, shipbroker Xclusiv said that “the product tanker market has experienced an extraordinary freight rally between early August and mid-October 2026, despite a significant contraction in global refined petroleum product trade. While declining cargo volumes would normally translate into weaker vessel demand and softer freight rates, the opposite has occurred. Refinery disruptions, geopolitical developments and changing vessel employment have created a market increasingly driven by tonnage availability and geographical imbalances rather than underlying cargo growth”. Source: Xclusiv shipbroker “According to Signal Ocean data, global seaborne refined product shipments declined by 10.9% year-on-year between 1 August and 15 October, falling from 265.96 million MT in 2025 to 237.07 million MT in 2026. Clean petroleum products accounted for most of this contraction, declining by 12.1% to 186.75 million MT, with naphtha recording the steepest reduction at 23.7%, followed by jet fuel at 14.5%, diesel at 10.3% and gasoline at 9.9%. Meanwhile, fuel oil shipments decreased by 5.8% to 50.32 million MT, highlighting the broader weakness in refined product transportation demand. Interestingly, this contraction has coincided with an exceptional strengthening in freight earnings. Between 3 August and 14 October, all 18 monitored Baltic Exchange product tanker routes registered gains, with LR2 and LR1 vessels leading the rally. The LR2 Middle East Gulf–UK Continent route (TC20) surged from USD 108,734/day to USD 324,060/day, an increase of 198%, while the LR1 equivalent (TC8) climbed 173% to USD 234,399/day. Similarly, the LR2 Middle East Gulf–Japan route (TC1) reached USD 284,762/day, compared to USD 138,253/day in early August. The Mediterranean–Far East LR2 route (TC15) recorded an even more remarkable 414% increase, reaching USD 172,513/day”, Xclusiv said. The shipbroker added that “the MR market has followed a similar upward trajectory, although geographical differences remain considerable. South Korea–Singapore (TC11) earnings increased by 261% to USD 64,144/day, while West Coast India–Japan (TC12) climbed 280% to USD 50,642/day. Singapore–Australia (TC7) strengthened by 188% to USD 67,775/day. Conversely, the Atlantic market experienced a less pronounced recovery, with US Gulf–UK Continent (TC14) increasing by just 35%, illustrating the stronger momentum across Eastern Hemisphere trades”. Meanwhile, according to Xclusiv, “a particularly important development is the changing employment pattern of larger product-capable tankers. During the examined period, Aframaxes engaged in crude trading increased by 20.3% year-on-year to 858 vessels, while crude-trading Panamaxes rose 18.6% to 134 units. Conversely, clean-trading LR2 participation declined by 39.2% to 158 vessels, while LR1 participation fell 9.6% to 208 units. With crude tanker earnings reaching exceptionally elevated levels, owners have increasingly found dirty trading more attractive, effectively withdrawing substantial capacity from the clean market. Importantly, returning these vessels to refined product transportation requires tank cleaning, preparation and additional time, preventing an immediate supply response”. Source: Xclusiv shipbroker “Looking ahead, geopolitical developments could further support this imbalance. The recent US–Russia agreement facilitating Russian diesel shipments, alongside Washington’s temporary sanctions relief, could generate additional product tanker employment and reshape trading routes. However, the actual increase in shipments remains uncertain. Should additional cargo demand materialise while LR vessels continue favouring lucrative crude employment, clean tanker availability could tighten further. Consequently, freight earnings may remain elevated despite declining overall trade volumes, with vessel deployment and geopolitical developments increasingly determining the market’s direction”, Xclusiv concluded. Nikos Roussanoglou, Hellenic Shipping News Worldwide Tops 2026-10-23 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.body: Global shipyard order book grows 13%, strengthening China’s lead in International Shipping News 23/10/2026 “O n 1 September 2026, the global shipyard order book reached an estimated 203.2m Compensated Gross Tonnage (CGT), up 13% from 180.0m CGT a year earlier,” says Niels Rasmussen, Chief Shipping Analyst at BIMCO. This is slightly below the all-time high of 210.4m CGT reached in May but remains above the previous record of 195.4m CGT from 2008. Much of the growth has been captured by Chinese shipyards, who secured 74% of the CGT contracted during the past year. This has further strengthened China’s position as the world’s largest shipbuilding nation. Chinese shipyards now hold 64% of the global order book while South Korean shipyards hold 19% and Japanese 6%. China’s dominance extends across the major cargo-carrying ship sectors. Its shipyards hold more than 72% of the order book in each of the six main sectors: container, tanker, gas tanker, dry bulk, other dry cargo and RoRo. Combined, these sectors account for 88% of the global order book. Their yards’ largest share is in the container ship segment, with 81% of the order book. “Container ships dominate both the order book and its growth over the past 12 months. They account for 30% of CGT on order and 68% of the increase during the past year,” says Rasmussen. Additionally, Chinese shipyards currently have better capacity coverage than their South Korean and Japanese competitors. If each shipyard’s current capacity is assumed to equal its highest annual CGT output during 2021–2025, Chinese shipyards hold orders equivalent to an average of 4.2 years of capacity. The corresponding figures for South Korean and Japanese yards are 1.9 and 1.7 years . Combined deliveries from China, South Korea and Japan peaked at 40.1m CGT in 2025, but 55.9m CGT and 60.0m CGT are currently scheduled for delivery in 2027 and 2028. Chinese yards, in particular, will have to raise output to manage the scheduled deliveries. Current capacity could therefore be assumed to equal the highest annual CGT delivered or scheduled for delivery during 2021–2030. In that case, average coverage falls to 2.1 years for Chinese shipyards and 1.6 years for both South Korean and Japanese shipyards. “China has further strengthened its position as the world’s leading shipbuilding nation, but its shipyards must raise annual output to new record highs in order to deliver. Chinese yards are scheduled to deliver a record 44.0m CGT in 2028, nearly twice the 22.7m CGT delivered in 2025. The capacity expansion needed to achieve this could increase the risk of underutilisation if contracting weakens in the future,” says Rasmussen. articles.body: The soaring cost of shipping is lifting the price of oil for consumers in International Shipping News 23/10/2026 D isruptions in the Middle East are pushing tanker rates to historic highs The price of oil is only part of what determines the cost to supply the world with fuel. Crude oil and the products refined from it must travel – often thousands of kilometres by specialised marine tankers – from producing regions and refining centres to the places where they are consumed. Typically, transport makes up a small proportion of the overall price of oil, but when shipping becomes more expensive, costs can mount across the supply chain. That pressure is now building across global oil markets, which have been repeatedly roiled by the war in the Middle East since February. While attention has focused on the availability of Gulf crude oil and the re-opening of trade routes through the Strait of Hormuz, freight costs have also soared in recent weeks – making it far more expensive to move crude and oil products around the world. In September, tanker rates surged to historic highs. By mid-October, the cost of shipping crude from the Middle East Gulf to Asia on a large tanker had climbed to over $37 per barrel, more than five times its level before the war began. For some refiners, especially those in Asia, these soaring transport costs can mean the difference between a profitable operation and a loss-making one. For economies heavily reliant on imports, higher freight rates add further upwards pressure on energy costs. A shipping bottleneck with global consequences Since the outbreak of the conflict, vessel congestion around the Strait of Hormuz, the rerouting of trade flows and growing use of ship-to-ship transfers have lengthened cargo delivery times and reduced fleet efficiency, driving freight rates higher. Under normal conditions, tankers travel between producers and consumers along established trade routes. The faster these journeys can be completed, the more oil the global fleet can transport. But rerouting cargoes or transferring them between ships ties up vessels for longer and reduces the number available for hire, causing freight rates to rise sharply. Shipping costs had already risen following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, which triggered a reshuffling of global crude and oil product trade. The rerouting of vessels following the European and G7 ban on Russian oil disrupted established trade flows. The increase in the number of vessels operating outside conventional shipping arrangements – the so-called shadow fleet, used to circumvent sanctions and carry Russian and Iranian oil – has reduced the pool of ships available to the wider market. The latest rally in freight rates followed a series of drone attacks on Saudi Arabia’s East-West crude oil pipeline on 11 September 2026. The pipeline has provided a critical bypass route for Saudi crude exports during the crisis, allowing oil to reach the Red Sea without having to pass through Hormuz. The temporary suspension of pipeline flows coincided with a ramp-up in Chinese buying, resulting in more Saudi oil moving through the Strait of Hormuz and pushing up demand for tankers. At the same time, the temporary loss of pipeline crude from the Saudi west coast left very large crude carriers (VLCCs) positioned at Sidi Kerir, off the coast of Egypt in the Mediterranean, without expected cargoes, forcing ship charterers to scramble for alternative crude supplies and vessels to transport them. This compounded an already tight freight market following the Houthis’ maritime blockade of Saudi navigation through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which had lengthened voyage times and reduced fleet efficiency. Saudi Arabia moved swiftly and effectively to repair and reopen the East-West Pipeline within a matter of days. However, these recent disruptions, combined with severely curtailed Saudi exports through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, mean that the repercussions are being felt at both ends of the oil trade. Importers face higher costs to receive crude and oil products, while exporters face downward pressure on the prices they receive for their oil. The effects are spreading across the global tanker market As vessels spend longer on disrupted routes, demand has spilled over into smaller tankers. Instead of using VLCCs, charterers have been splitting crude cargoes across smaller Suezmax and Aframax vessels, driving up demand for both. In the third quarter of 2026, demand for these two tanker classes, measured on a tonne-mile basis – which accounts for both the volume of cargo transported and the distance it travels – was around 20% higher than a year earlier. By mid-October, shipping crude from West Africa to Europe on a Suezmax vessel cost over $22 per barrel, more than four times pre-conflict levels. North Sea Aframax rates also tripled, reaching over $6 per barrel. Freight rate impact on oil refining profitability in Singapore, 2026 VLCC= very large crude carrier. This chart shows the indicative refining margin for a refinery with a catalytic cracking configuration operating in Singapore, as per the IEA refining margins calculation. The freight rate displayed is for a VLCC loading in the Middle East Gulf and delivering to Asia Pacific. IEA analysis based on data from Argus Media Group. The impact has extended into the product tanker market. Exceptionally high earnings in crude shipping have encouraged some owners to use Long Range 2 (LR2) vessels – the largest tankers commonly used for long-haul shipments of oil products – to transport crude instead. As a result, oil product cargoes have been redistributed across the fleet of smaller vessels, tightening shipping capacity throughout the product tanker market. Freight rates for Long Range 1 (LR1) tankers travelling from the Middle East Gulf to Japan were nearly $27 per barrel in mid-October, five times higher than before the conflict. Further disruptions to global oil trade could tighten tanker markets even more. The prospect of a US diesel export ban added to concerns of further trade dislocation in September. Such a measure would have reduced demand for tankers in the Atlantic Basin but increased the need for longer-distance shipments from Asia to Europe and Latin America. Refiners face a narrowing set of options The most significant impact of record-high freight rates on refining profitability has been in Asia, where refiners depend heavily on Middle Eastern crude. They have faced some of the highest transport costs as cargoes are shuttled through the Strait of Hormuz to secondary tankers for onward delivery to Asia. By mid-October, charter rates for VLCCs on the Middle East Gulf-to-Asia route had soared to over $1.3 million a day. At such high levels, shipping costs can erode the value refiners would otherwise earn from processing crude into oil products. In September, this surge in delivered crude costs pushed margins for Asian refiners processing crude from the Middle East into negative territory. Until recently, robust refining margins in Europe allowed refiners to absorb substantially higher transport costs. However, the rise in crude prices during the second half of September also started to strain their profitability. Refiners can try to limit their exposure by buying alternative crude grades, including lighter, lower-sulphur oil from the United States. But shipping costs have risen on those routes too. By mid-October, transporting crude from the US Gulf Coast to Singapore cost around $33 per barrel, while the cost to move crude to Europe was $24 per barrel, over four times pre-conflict levels. This leaves many refiners facing difficult choices: accept sharply higher costs for the crude they process, switch to less optimal crude grades that may reduce product yields, or cut operating rates. The last option could further tighten global supplies of diesel, kerosene and other oil products, adding upward pressure to prices and hence on consumers. Restoring oil production and a full reopening of the Strait of Hormuz will be essential to easing the disruption to oil markets. However, even if security conditions in the Gulf improve, high export volumes, efforts to rebuild depleted crude oil and oil product stocks and persistent inefficiencies in shipping routes could continue to constrain tanker availability and keep shipping rates elevated for some time. takeaways: Crude oil and the products refined from it must travel – often thousands of kilometres by specialised marine tankers – from producing regions and refining centres to the places where they are consumed.
Typically, transport makes up a small proportion of the overall price of oil, but when shipping becomes more expensive, costs can mount across the supply chain.
That pressure is now building across global oil markets, which have been repeatedly roiled by the war in the Middle East since February.

articles.title: New report reveals China’s key strengths across green shipping corridor building blocks
articles.summary: A new report from the Global Maritime Forum reveals that China has quickly become a global leader in green shipping corridors, with nearly one-fifth of the world’s corridor initiatives connecting to a Chinese port. Launched today at the Global Maritime Forum’s Annual Summit 2026 in Shanghai, ‘Green shipping...
articles.body: New report reveals China’s key strengths across green shipping corridor building blocks in International Shipping News , Shipping: Emission Possible 23/10/2026 A new report from the Global Maritime Forum reveals that China has quickly become a global leader in green shipping corridors, with nearly one-fifth of the world’s corridor initiatives connecting to a Chinese port. Launched today at the Global Maritime Forum’s Annual Summit 2026 in Shanghai, ‘Green shipping corridors: How China is re-energising the global movement’ measures China’s progress against the four key building blocks considered crucial to successfully starting up a green corridor. The report finds that China is one of the strongest actors globally in this space, holding strategic advantages in three of the four building blocks. “The Global Maritime Forum has been measuring global progress on green corridors since 2022, when China was involved in three announced initiatives—now, that number has risen to more than 20,” said Jesse Fahnestock, director of decarbonisation at the Global Maritime Forum. “China’s advancements on green fuel development and efforts around international collaboration could be success factors for these initiatives.” First introduced in a 2021 report for the Getting to Zero Coalition, the concept of the four building blocks remains a useful tool for benchmarking corridor viability: • Viable zero-emission fuel and technology pathways: Availability of zero-emission fuels, technologies, and bunkering infrastructure to service zero-emission vessels. • Cross-value-chain collaboration: Stakeholders committed to decarbonisation and willing to explore new forms of collaboration from both demand and supply sides. • Enabling policy environment: Policy incentives and regulations that narrow the cost gap and expedite safety measures. • Customer demand: Conditions need to be in place to mobilise demand for green shipping and scale zero-emission shipping on the corridor. China’s performance across the first three building blocks is strong; it is an early and cost-competitive producer of green methanol and ammonia, is at the forefront of marine battery development, is highly engaged in cross-value chain collaborations, and is rapidly strengthening its policies related to green hydrogen. As is the case in many countries, the report reveals that customer demand for China’s zero-emission fuels (the fourth building block) is lagging behind the levels needed to match its potential supply. However, the report outlines multiple opportunities for China to better mobilise demand, including using policy mechanisms to close the cost gap and further advance infrastructure for methanol, ammonia, and battery electric ships. “China has the opportunity to leverage its existing strengths across the building blocks to incentivise early adoption, foster collaboration, and develop necessary infrastructure,” Fahnestock said. “Even in the time since this report was finished, we’ve seen multiple announcements of progress in these areas, which is highly encouraging.” Source: Global Maritime Forum 2026-10-23 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

• Cross-value-chain collaboration: Stakeholders committed to decarbonisation and willing to explore new forms of collaboration from both demand and supply sides.
• Enabling policy environment: Policy incentives and regulations that narrow the cost gap and expedite safety measures.

articles.title: Titan analysis shows FuelEU pooling propelled liquefied biomethane demand
articles.summary: Titan, part of Molgas, has analysed the role of LNG, liquefied biomethane (LBM/bio-LNG) and e-methane (the methane decarbonisation pathway) in FuelEU Maritime compliance, as well as the performance of the regulation, particularly its pooling mechanism, so far. The paper models compliance for an 8,000 TEU...
articles.body: Titan analysis shows FuelEU pooling propelled liquefied biomethane demand in International Shipping News , Shipping: Emission Possible 23/10/2026 Titan, part of Molgas, has analysed the role of LNG, liquefied biomethane (LBM/bio-LNG) and e-methane (the methane decarbonisation pathway) in FuelEU Maritime compliance, as well as the performance of the regulation, particularly its pooling mechanism, so far. The paper models compliance for an 8,000 TEU containership operating a route spanning Rotterdam, Antwerp, Hamburg and Algeciras using approximately 18,000 metric tons of LNG-equivalent fuel annually, all within the scope of FuelEU Maritime. Three scenarios are shown: a fuel oil baseline, grey LNG, and a 30% LBM blend. The oil-fuelled vessel is in deficit in 2025, and penalty costs grow steeply from ~€2.2M to ~€17M by 2040 as targets tighten. With LNG, the containership generates overcompliance of 11,700 tCO₂eq per year in 2025 and remains compliant through 2035. From 2040, a typical 15% LBM blend restores compliance, and any extra LBM generates surplus pooling value. Introducing a 30% LBM blend can increase that surplus to over 34,000 tCO₂eq annually. That represents ~€3.4M to ~€5.1M per year in gross transferable compliance value. The figures use FuelEU Maritime’s default well-to-wake emissions factor, covering the fuel’s full lifecycle, together with the published penalty rate of €2,400 per ton VLSFO energy equivalent. Gross pooling values are indicative, based on a market range of €100–150/ tCO₂eq. The net commercial benefit will depend on the market compliance values negotiated and the cost premium of LBM versus fossil LNG. For customers, Titan can model this precisely for each ship and supply scenario. MSC Viola boxship bunkering with Titan chartered United LNG I Grégoire Hartig, Commercial Director at Titan, commented: “Pooling effectively converts over-achieving emissions performance targets into a tradable or allocatable asset. This bridges the market and competition-based nature of maritime transport with the implementation of stringent greenhouse gas regulation. This has, in our view, proven to be a very efficient way to ensure the active participation and alignment of all stakeholders. “In large part due to ship operators seeking FuelEU Maritime overcompliance, we have already recorded LBM rising from 6.5% to 19.1% of our total delivered volume of methane from 2024 to 2025. LBM prices have been high in 2026 so far, we expect a better second half to the year. Let’s not forget, though, that 2025 has only been the first year where FuelEU pools have been implemented, and that, through iteration, the role of LBM and its impact on compliance values will become clearer.” Maro Varvate, Commercial Manager at Titan, said: “FuelEU offers a strategic, practical and cost-effective approach to decarbonisation and fleet renewal, which takes into account the lifecycle of maritime asset investment. If ship operators are pooling their own ships, it allows them to target and sequence decarbonisation investments pragmatically, improving selected vessels first while maintaining compliance across their fleet. “This targeted approach also makes sense from a fuel supply point of view. It allows LNG, and particularly LBM as it continues to scale up, to be efficiently produced and supplied to one ship in one location, and yet the benefits can be shared over the wider shipping service. This also enables demand to incrementally scale up as profits are being made from over-compliant vessels.” Grégoire Hartig, Commercial Director, Titan Clean Fuels Beyond pooling, the paper argues that the EU’s well-to-tank default emissions factor for LNG is too high. It cites Rystad Energy’s LNG ‘Well-To-Tank Emissions Assessment 2025’ report, where the global well-to-tank emissions intensity of LNG used as bunker fuel in 2024 was shown to be 13.9 g CO2e/MJ (LHV), below the current EU well-to-tank default of 18.5 gCO2e/MJ. Titan also discusses the journey that the LNG Industry has been on in reducing methane slip and upstream supply chain leakage. It calls on regulators to reward good performance and penalise poor performance, highlighting that the current generic default emissions factor offers almost no compliance or financial incentive for shipowners to choose engine technology with minimal slip and use LNG with lower-emission supply chains. This FuelEU Maritime analysis follows the conclusion of Titan’s first year managing its own pool, which has been verified by DNV and positively includes several hundred vessels. It has taken full responsibility for the compliance balance and monitoring, optimising overcompliance based on market dynamics and leveraging its own access to LNG and LBM. Source: Titan Clean Fuels 2026-10-23 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share
takeaways: Three scenarios are shown: a fuel oil baseline, grey LNG, and a 30% LBM blend.
The oil-fuelled vessel is in deficit in 2025, and penalty costs grow steeply from ~€2.2M to ~€17M by 2040 as targets tighten.
With LNG, the containership generates overcompliance of 11,700 tCO₂eq per year in 2025 and remains compliant through 2035.

articles.title: Ports encouraged to prepare now for advanced nuclear in maritime and clean energy
articles.summary: Ports should begin structured planning for advanced nuclear technology now, treating it as a long-term infrastructure and operating-model question rather than a new marine fuel, according to a new joint paper from the British Ports Association (BPA) and Lloyd’s Register (LR). Advanced Nuclear Technology Use Within...
articles.body: Ports encouraged to prepare now for advanced nuclear in maritime and clean energy in International Shipping News 23/10/2026 Ports should begin structured planning for advanced nuclear technology now, treating it as a long-term infrastructure and operating-model question rather than a new marine fuel, according to a new joint paper from the British Ports Association (BPA) and Lloyd’s Register (LR). Advanced Nuclear Technology Use Within Port Environments outlines how nuclear could support ports’ growing demand for reliable, low-carbon power while creating new maritime and industrial opportunities. Potential applications include nuclear-powered ship calls, floating or transportable nuclear power units, and land-based small modular reactors or microreactors to power port operations and support fuel production. The report finds that the most significant barriers are not solely technical. Regulatory alignment, governance, emergency preparedness, liability, insurance, workforce capability and public confidence will all be critical to safe and commercially viable deployment. It calls on ports to integrate nuclear scenarios into their established marine safety-management systems, rather than create a parallel regime. Existing disciplines used to manage dangerous goods, hazardous cargoes, security zones and high-consequence operations provide a strong foundation, but will need additional nuclear-specific evidence, competence, monitoring and regulatory interfaces. For ports, the opportunity extends beyond accommodating nuclear-powered vessels. Advanced reactors could provide baseload electricity for port estates, shore power, cargo-handling equipment, cold storage and neighbouring industry, as well as heat and electricity for hydrogen and synthetic fuel production. Ports could also develop high-value capabilities in shipbuilding, reactor-module integration, inspection, maintenance, specialist logistics and decommissioning. Keith Johnstone, LR’s Director of Strategic Partnerships, Nuclear, at the British Ports Association Annual Conference in Dover Mark Tipping, Global Offshore Power-to-X Director at Lloyd’s Register, said: “Advanced nuclear has the potential to transform ports from energy consumers into resilient, low-carbon energy and industrial hubs. But realising that opportunity will depend on more than technology alone. Ports need to further assess governance, proportionate assurance and early collaboration across the maritime and nuclear sectors. By starting that work now, port leaders can build the evidence, capability and public confidence needed to make informed decisions as the market develops.” Richard Ballantyne, Chief Executive at BPA, said: “For ports, the opportunities for advanced nuclear go beyond receiving a nuclear-powered ship. They are already planning for significant changes in energy demand, infrastructure and the vessels they serve. Advanced nuclear may not be the right solution for every port, but it is important that the sector understands the potential applications and starts asking the right questions early on.” The paper proposes a tiered readiness model, enabling each port to adopt a proportionate level of ambition: from becoming ‘nuclear-aware’, with the ability to assess enquiries and engage authorities, through to ‘nuclear-ready’ and ‘nuclear-enabled’, or ultimately operating as a nuclear energy hub. Recommended no-regret actions include mapping stakeholders, assessing future energy demand and grid constraints, engaging regulators early and preparing clear, evidence-led communications for workforces and local communities. The report also sets out a staged pathway from initial orientation and feasibility assessment to development and delivery. This is designed to help ports build evidence and confidence before major capital is committed, recognising that advanced nuclear will not be appropriate for every location. International regulation remains a central challenge. Existing maritime nuclear frameworks pre-date today’s advanced reactor designs, while nuclear and maritime safety regimes are often insufficiently integrated. The paper highlights the importance of ports, governments, regulators, classification societies, insurers and technology developers working together to clarify responsibilities and shape workable national and international approaches. Recent port-focused work, including the assessment of a nuclear-powered feeder containership calling at the Port of Rotterdam, indicates that nuclear ship calls can be considered through safety themes already familiar to ports, provided nuclear-specific requirements are incorporated systematically. The BPA and LR conclude that preparation should precede procurement. Ports that begin proportionate planning now will be better placed to make informed investment decisions, maintain public confidence and influence the regulatory and commercial frameworks that will determine nuclear’s role in the next generation of maritime infrastructure. Source: Lloyd’s Register (LR) 2026-10-23 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

Potential applications include nuclear-powered ship calls, floating or transportable nuclear power units, and land-based small modular reactors or microreactors to power port operations and support fuel production.

articles.summary: North America Bunker demand is strong at the US Gulf port of Houston, where all three conventional grades are tight for prompt supply. articles.body: ENGINE: Americas Bunker Fuel Availability Outlook in International Shipping News 23/10/2026 North America Bunker demand is strong at the US Gulf port of Houston, where all three conventional grades are tight for prompt supply. Recommended lead times across HSFO, VLSFO and LSMGO run from more than five days to a week, and some suppliers may ask for more than seven days, depending on the size of the enquiry, a trader said. Vessel traffic through the Houston Ship Channel will face night-time closures from late December, when construction begins on a new bridge at Beltway 8, a ship agency said. Ships will not be allowed to transit beneath the bridge while a closure is in force. The closures are expected to run every other night from 1800 to 0400 hrs local time, and to continue for the next 4-5 months. At the Galveston Offshore Lightering Area (GOLA) anchorage, availability for all three fuel grades is tight this week. Recommended lead times are stretched to 6-8 days, a source said. Rough weather at the anchorage can lead to further delays in deliveries. Sea fog poses a low threat to visibility at Galveston through Wednesday. However, at Corpus Christi, fog is expected to turn moderate on next Tuesday with visibility dropping to around 4 nautical miles. The fog threat is also low across the rest of the US Gulf coast, at Brownsville, Corpus Christi, Freeport, Port Arthur, Lake Charles, Marsh Island, Port Fourchon, New Orleans, Venice, Pascagoula, Mobile Bay and Tampa. Bunker demand has increased at New York over the week, a source tells ENGINE. Availability for prompt supply of VLSFO and HSFO is tight, with both grades needing more than five days. LSMGO is in better supply, with recommended lead times of 2-3 days. Northerly winds of 15-20 knots have eased to 10-15 knots late this morning, with waves of 2-4 feet and occasional 5 feet seas. Conditions are expected to settle after that, with winds falling to around 5 knots and backing to the west, and waves of 1 foot or less. Two tropical systems are active, but neither is expected to threaten bunker operations in the region. Subtropical Storm Josephine is several hundred miles off the US east coast and is accelerating northeastward away from the coast, with maximum sustained winds of 55 knots. The US National Hurricane Center expects it to turn into a powerful extratropical cyclone, a storm that draws its energy from clashing air masses rather than warm sea water, as it moves further out into the North Atlantic. In the eastern Pacific, Tropical Storm Vance is well off Mexico’s Pacific coast, moving west with winds of 45 knots. Marine warnings are in effect for parts of the eastern Pacific. On the US west coast, the bunker market at Los Angeles and Long Beach is steady. Availability is normal at the two ports, with most suppliers able to deliver VLSFO and HSFO in 5-7 days. LSMGO can be delivered in under five days. Latin America and the Caribbean Bunker availability has tightened across all three grades at the ports of Balboa and Cristobal in Panama, and fuel demand is reported to be muted. Suppliers need more than a week to deliver VLSFO and LSMGO stems. HSFO is the most tight, with suppliers recommending lead times of 8-10 days. Panama’s bunker sales fell by around 7% in September from August, with HSFO volumes sliding to their lowest monthly level since July 2023. In Colombia, HSFO availability is tight at Cartagena and can be arranged only under prior consultation with suppliers, a trader said. VLSFO and LSMGO are in better supply at Cartagena, Barranquilla and Santa Marta, where the earliest delivery dates for both grades fall 3-4 days out, the trader added. HSFO is also tight at Peru’s Callao and available only under prior consultation. VLSFO and LSMGO availability is normal at the port, with recommended lead times of 5-7 days, a trader said. In Brazil, VLSFO and LSMGO availability is normal at Santos, where lead times are 4-7 days this week. Rio de Janeiro can supply HSFO, but only under prior consultation. VLSFO and LSMGO availability is normal at the port, and both grades require lead times of 4-7 days. Paranagua, Belem and Vila do Conde have all maintained normal availability of VLSFO and LSMGO, with recommended lead times of 3-7 days across the three ports, a source said. Further south at Rio Grande, the earliest delivery date for VLSFO is 25 October. LSMGO is not available at the port. VLSFO and LSMGO remain tight in Argentina’s Zona Comun, where lead times at the anchorage are 8-10 days. Source: By Gautamee Hazarika, ENGINE, https://www.engine.online/news 2026-10-23 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.body: Hapag-Lloyd expects more shipping services to return to Suez Canal in International Shipping News 23/10/2026 Hamburg-based shipping company Hapag-Lloyd expects additional services to resume transits through the Suez Canal, joining two services already operating to and from Asia, according to a statement from the Suez Canal Authority (SCA). The anticipated return was discussed during a meeting between Ossama Rabiee, Chairman and Managing Director of the SCA, and Juan Pablo Richards, Hapag-Lloyd’s Senior Managing Director for Region South Europe. Held at the SCA’s headquarters in the Irshad Building in Ismailia, the meeting explored cooperation to increase traffic through the canal. Richards explained that Hapag-Lloyd is closely monitoring developments in the Red Sea and maritime safety indicators to guide changes to its sailing schedules as transits gradually resume through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait and the Suez Canal. He expressed hope that the improvement in canal traffic indicators would continue. Rabiee affirmed the canal’s readiness to accommodate returning shipping services, pointing to the SCA’s ongoing development of maritime services and modernization of its fleet to meet customers’ changing requirements. He expressed hope for the full resumption of Hapag-Lloyd’s services through the canal, emphasizing the waterway’s importance to maintaining global supply chains amid geopolitical challenges and rapid changes in the shipping industry. The discussions also addressed potential cooperation beyond shipping operations. Richards identified an opportunity for the SCA’s Maritime Training and Simulation Academy to work with the Damietta Alliance Container Terminal, also known as Tahya Misr 1, at Damietta Port on training for Ship Captains. Hapag-Lloyd is a major investor in the terminal. Earlier, Denmark-based shipping group A.P. Moller-Maersk announced that it expects all its shipping services to return to the Suez Canal by March 2027. Source: Arab Finance 2026-10-23 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.title: MPA marks christening of first ammonia dual-fuelled vessel
articles.summary: The Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore and Eastern Pacific Shipping have marked the christening of Terra Clove at HD Hyundai Heavy Industries in Ulsan, South Korea. The 93,000 cubic metre Very Large Ammonia Carrier is EPS’s first ammonia dual-fuelled vessel and the first ammonia dual-fuelled commercial newbuild...
articles.body: The Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore and Eastern Pacific Shipping have marked the christening of Terra Clove at HD Hyundai Heavy Industries in Ulsan, South Korea. The 93,000 cubic metre Very Large Ammonia Carrier is EPS’s first ammonia dual-fuelled vessel and the first ammonia dual-fuelled commercial newbuild vessel to be registered under the Singapore Registry of Ships. The vessel is equipped with Everllence’s first commercial ammonia dual-fuelled two-stroke marine engine, which successfully completed factory acceptance testing in April 2026. Delivery is expected in November 2026 following upcoming sea trials. Terra Clove is the result of a collaboration initiated in June 2022 by MPA, EPS, HHI and the American Bureau of Shipping to develop an ammonia dual-fuelled gas carrier under the Singapore flag. It is the first of two such vessels being built by HHI for EPS, both of which will be registered under the Singapore flag. Designed to transport ammonia as cargo and use it as propulsion fuel, the vessel incorporates specialised ammonia fuel handling, containment and safety systems. As Singapore’s flag administration, MPA worked closely with EPS, HHI, ABS and other industry partners on technical and regulatory compliance, reviewing the vessel’s design against IMO guidelines, participating in hazard identification and operability studies and providing regulatory guidance on ammonia detection, fuel system safety and emissions management. MPA also shared experience from earlier ammonia trials to support the development of onboard safety procedures and crew preparedness. Ang Wee Keong, Chief Executive of MPA, described Terra Clove as demonstrating that bringing together expertise from across the maritime value chain can address the uncertainties and investment risks inherent in new technology development, expressing hope that the vessel’s successful development will give the wider industry greater confidence in ammonia as a marine fuel. Cyril Ducau, CEO of EPS, described the naming as an important milestone toward making ammonia a viable marine fuel, emphasising that safe and practical operation remains the priority alongside technology development.

articles.body: DSV reported higher revenue and operating profit in the third quarter of 2026, supported by strong earnings in its Air & Sea and Contract Logistics divisions. Revenue reached DKK 80.7 billion, compared with DKK 72 billion in the same period last year. Operating profit (EBIT) before special items increased to DKK 6.6 billion from DKK 5.4 billion. The quarterly result included DKK 300 million in gains from property disposals. Despite the earnings growth, DSV faced operational challenges in its European Road division following the integration of Schenker. Air & Sea and Contract Logistics support earnings DSV’s Air & Sea division reported EBIT before special items of DKK 4.28 billion, up 18.9% year-on-year. The improvement was mainly driven by cost savings from the Schenker integration. The division’s conversion ratio increased to 45.8%, compared with 38.6% a year earlier. Contract Logistics also delivered strong results, with operating profit rising 50.3% to DKK 1.67 billion. The division benefited from integration synergies, higher productivity and better warehouse capacity utilisation. Its results included DKK 105 million in property disposal gains. In contrast, Road division operating profit declined 35.1% to DKK 526 million, including DKK 195 million from property disposals. DSV attributed the decline to lower productivity and falling volumes following service disruptions linked to the Schenker integration. However, the company said Road operations had returned to normal by the end of September. However, some remaining savings in the Road division and certain Group functions are now expected to be realised in 2027. The company has also narrowed its full-year 2026 guidance for EBIT before special items to DKK 24–25 billion, compared with its previous range of DKK 23.5–25.5 billion. “We delivered earnings growth in a volatile market, driven by strong results in Air & Sea and Contract Logistics,” said Jens H. Lund, Group CEO of DSV. Meanwhile, DSV announced a new DKK 1.5 billion share buyback programme, its first since acquiring Schenker. The programme begins on October 21, 2026, and will run until February 1, 2027.

articles.title: Port of Los Angeles Reports Record Low Emissions
articles.summary: The Port of Los Angeles recorded its lowest emissions per container on record in 2025, continuing a two-decade decline in air pollution even as container throughput remained near historic highs.According to the port's newly released Inventory of Air Emissions…
articles.body: Port of Los Angeles Reports Record Low Emissions Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 22, 2026 Image courtesy Port of Los Angeles The Port of Los Angeles recorded its lowest emissions per container on record in 2025, continuing a two-decade decline in air pollution even as container throughput remained near historic highs. According to the port's newly released Inventory of Air Emissions, diesel particulate matter (DPM) emissions declined 2% in 2025 compared with 2024, while nitrogen oxides (NOx) fell 4%, sulfur oxides (SOx) decreased 5% and greenhouse gas emissions dropped 3%. The NOx reduction brought annual emissions to their lowest level since the port began tracking air pollution in 2005. The improvements came as Los Angeles handled nearly 10.2 million twenty-foot equivalent units (TEUs), maintaining its position as the nation's busiest container port. Since 2005, the port has reduced DPM emissions by 90%, NOx by 72%, SOx by 98% and greenhouse gases by 16%, while container volumes increased 37%. Much of the progress reflects investments in cleaner vessels, cargo-handling equipment and landside transportation. Ocean-going vessels have reduced DPM emissions by 94% and SOx by 98% since 2005, aided by cleaner fuels, shore power and emissions capture technologies. Harbor craft are also contributing. In 2025, 55% of tugs, barges, ferries and other workboats met Tier 3 or Tier 4 emissions standards, compared with 20% in 2017. Harbor craft DPM emissions have fallen 69% since 2005. Electric cargo-handling equipment increased 20% during 2025, with zero-emission units now representing 14% of the port's equipment fleet. Meanwhile, truck-related DPM and NOx emissions declined 16% and 25%, respectively, year over year. "These results demonstrate that we can move high cargo volumes while continuing to reduce emissions," said Port Executive Director Gene Seroka. The findings reflect ongoing implementation of the San Pedro Bay ports' Clean Air Action Plan, including investments in zero-emission equipment, charging infrastructure and cleaner maritime operations.

October 22, 2026 © Crewsure Insurance Services Limited Crewsure Insurance Services Limited (Crewsure) has announced the launch of Crewsure Energy, a new program that brings together traditional employee benefits with specialist Crisis Response protection, designed for companies employing personnel working in the international energy and offshore sectors. The launch represents an expansion for Crewsure, as the company already provides specialist MLC crew benefits for personnel working aboard drilling ships and other maritime assets. Crewsure Energy now extends that expertise beyond the vessel to provide dedicated protection for employees and contractors working on offshore rigs and other declared energy operations. At its core are emergency medical expenses, personal accident and wages protection, with worldwide cover available subject to the policy terms and schedule. The medical section covers medical emergency treatment following illness or accident, while personal accident protection includes accidental death and permanent disability benefits and loss of wages cover and loss of baggage. The program also recognizes the operational consequences for an employer when a member of an overseas workforce can no longer continue their assignment. Cover can therefore include reasonable additional costs of recruiting and sending a replacement employee overseas following death, illness, bodily injury or qualifying compulsory quarantine. A distinguishing feature of Crewsure Energy is its integrated Crisis Response protection. Rather than treating employee benefits and security risks entirely separately, the program can respond to events including kidnap, detention, disappearance, hijack, hostage crisis, extortion, threats and virtual kidnap, with access to professional response consultants. Crisis benefits can extend considerably beyond the immediate incident, including response consultant costs, travel and accommodation, loss of salary, replacement key-person costs, legal and medical expenses, rehabilitation and job retraining, temporary security measures and other specified additional expenses. The program can also provide Emergency Political Repatriation and Relocation and Threat Repatriation, including specified travel and accommodation costs and, in qualifying circumstances, personal effects left behind and irrevocably lost following an emergency political repatriation. Emergency medical, inpatient and evacuation/repatriation assistance is supported by Northcott Global Solutions, with 24-hour assistance available, while the Crisis Response section provides access to specialist response consultants. articles.body: Shipbuilding: Bayonne Drydock Gets MARAD Grant Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 22, 2026 Members of Bayonne Drydock’s Executive Leadership Team pose with Congressman Rob Menendez, NJ State Senator Angela McKnight, NJ Assemblyman Jerry Walker, Mayor Sharon Nadrowski, and Bayonne City Council Image courtesy BDD Bayonne Drydock & Repair Corp. has secured a $673,123 grant from the U.S. Maritime Administration (MARAD) to upgrade surface preparation equipment and expand workforce training at its ship repair facility in the Port of New York and New Jersey. Awarded through MARAD's Small Shipyard Grant Program , the funding will be combined with the shipyard's own investment to purchase automated ultra-high-pressure hydro-blasting and surface preparation equipment. The improvements are intended to increase productivity, reduce vessel turnaround times and enhance the yard's ability to service commercial and government vessels. The investment includes an integrated robotic hydro-blasting system, an additional surface preparation unit and supporting spare parts. "This vital federal investment allows us to modernize our surface-preparation infrastructure with state-of-the-art robotic technology," said Ryan Patrick Woerner, Executive Vice President and General Counsel of Bayonne Drydock. Woerner said the additional equipment will improve operational productivity, limit downtime and provide employees with tools to support maritime readiness. The latest award continues a series of MARAD-supported capital improvements at the Bayonne facility. In 2018, the shipyard received $1.08 million for upgrades to its graving dock and welding equipment. Another $730,477 grant followed in 2023 for hydro-blasting equipment and telehandlers. Founded in 1997, Bayonne Drydock operates a full-service repair facility at the former Military Ocean Terminal in Bayonne, New Jersey. Its principal infrastructure includes a 1,092-foot graving dock and a 1,280-metric-ton mobile boat hauler. Join the leading maritime news network Photo courtesy SUNY Maritime College SUNY Maritime College’s training ship Empire State VII is expected to return to its Fort Schuyler campus by mid-November after the federal government abruptly changed plans for a months-long deployment supporting the U.S. Navy. The reversal comes just weeks after the vessel departed New York for Norfolk, Virginia, where it was scheduled to undergo maintenance and flight deck certification ahead of a classified national security mission. In an October 21 message to the college community, SUNY Maritime President Rear Admiral John A. Okon confirmed the change. “I am pleased to share an important update on Empire State VII. The federal activation plan has changed, and the ship is now expected to return to Fort Schuyler for academic use, ship work, and with watches resuming no later than the middle of November,” Okon wrote. The announcement marks a significant shift from the original plans outlined by the U.S. Maritime Administration (MARAD), which ordered the vessel’s activation in August for an anticipated 170-day federal mission. An August 28 decision memorandum reviewed by gCaptain said the ship was needed to meet an urgent Military Sealift Command requirement and that no other suitable vessel was available within the required timeframe. Maritime Administrator Stephen Carmel described the activation as a “compelling strategic necessity.” The ship subsequently departed New York for Norfolk on September 30, with plans to remain there through October 30 for maintenance and flight deck certification ahead of follow-on operations supporting the Navy. The nature and destination of those operations were never publicly disclosed. It remains unclear what prompted the change in plans, whether the original military requirement has been withdrawn or reassigned, or how much of the planned work in Norfolk has been completed. For SUNY Maritime, however, the early return is welcome news. The vessel’s absence had threatened to disrupt academic programs, shipboard training and the sea time cadets need to qualify for U.S. Coast Guard licenses. “Empire State is more than a training ship. It is a classroom, a laboratory, and an essential part of the Maritime experience,” Okon said. Okon previously warned that losing the ship for much of the academic year would create significant challenges, and he pressed MARAD to return the vessel by February to keep the college’s 2027 Summer Sea Term on schedule. The revised timeline would bring the ship home roughly three months earlier than that requested deadline. Empire State VII , delivered in 2023, is the first of five purpose-built National Security Multi-Mission Vessels (NSMVs) developed by MARAD. The ships are designed primarily to train future merchant marine officers while also providing the federal government with additional sealift and emergency response capabilities. The vessel’s activation was expected to provide an early test of the NSMV program’s dual-use concept, demonstrating how a federally owned training ship could be called into service for national security missions. Instead, the shortened deployment raises questions about the circumstances behind the original urgent military requirement and the subsequent decision to release the vessel. “We will continue working with MARAD to confirm the exact details of the ship’s return and ensure we are ready to resume normal operations,” Okon said. articles.title: Panama Canal transits rise 4.1% in FY2026 as tonnage reaches 521 million
articles.summary: The Panama Canal recorded higher vessel traffic and tonnage in fiscal year 2026, supported by stronger activity in energy shipping and the container shipping sector. The waterway handled 13,951 vessel transits between October 2025 and September 2026, an increase of 4.1% compared with 13,404 transits in the previous...
articles.body: The Panama Canal recorded higher vessel traffic and tonnage in fiscal year 2026, supported by stronger activity in energy shipping and the container shipping sector. The waterway handled 13,951 vessel transits between October 2025 and September 2026, an increase of 4.1% compared with 13,404 transits in the previous fiscal year. Total tonnage reached 521 million Panama Canal Universal Measurement System (PC/UMS) tons, up 6.5% from 489.2 million PC/UMS tons in FY2025. The Panama Canal Authority reported the results on October 21, highlighting continued demand for the waterway and improved operating conditions. Neopanamax traffic supports growth Larger vessels contributed to the canal’s performance during the year. Ships using the Neopanamax locks accounted for 52.2% of total PC/UMS tonnage. Tonnage through these locks increased by 8.2% compared with the previous fiscal year. The canal also maintained a maximum permitted draft of 50 feet throughout the dry season, supporting vessel operations despite ongoing water management challenges. Meanwhile, total revenue increased by 16.6% to approximately $6.6 billion. The Panama Canal Authority noted that these financial figures remain unaudited. The authority continues to advance its long-term development plans under Vision 2025–2035, including the Río Indio Lake Project. Last-minute transit reservations restored Alongside its annual results, the Panama Canal Authority announced the immediate reinstatement of its Last-Minute Reservation service for vessels using the Panamax locks. The service provides ships without an existing reservation with another opportunity to secure a transit slot when capacity becomes available. However, the allocation of these slots remains at the canal authority’s discretion. The decision follows improvements in water management and recent rainfall levels approaching historical averages in the canal’s watershed. The authority said it will continue monitoring water conditions and announce further operational adjustments when necessary. The latest results reflect increased canal activity, while the return of last-minute reservations provides additional flexibility for shipping companies planning transits through the waterway.

articles.body: Hapag-Lloyd expects additional shipping services to return to the Suez Canal as maritime conditions in the Red Sea gradually improve, according to the Suez Canal Authority (SCA). The development was discussed during a meeting between SCA Chairman Adm. Ossama Rabiee and Juan Pablo Richards, Hapag-Lloyd’s Regional Head for Southern Europe, on October 21. These assessments will guide decisions on possible adjustments to sailing schedules as vessel traffic gradually returns through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait and the Suez Canal. Meanwhile, Rabiee reaffirmed the canal’s readiness to accommodate returning shipping services. He also expressed hope that Hapag-Lloyd would eventually restore all its services through the waterway. The SCA chairman highlighted ongoing improvements to navigation services and the authority’s fleet, aimed at meeting the operational requirements of shipping companies. Further cooperation discussed Beyond vessel transits, the two sides explored opportunities to expand their cooperation. Richards expressed interest in potential collaboration between the SCA’s Maritime Training and Simulation Academy and the Damietta Alliance Container Handling Terminal, also known as Tahya Misr 1, at Damietta Port. The proposed cooperation would focus on training ship masters, reflecting Hapag-Lloyd’s involvement as a major investor in the Damietta Alliance Terminal. The discussions come as shipping companies continue evaluating the security and operational conditions required for a broader return to the Suez Canal route. While Hapag-Lloyd anticipates additional services returning, the company has not announced a confirmed schedule for further route changes.

articles.summary: China has further cemented its dominance of global shipbuilding, capturing nearly three-quarters of new orders over the past year as the industry’s order book approaches record levels, according to new...

Photo courtesy OOCL China has further cemented its dominance of global shipbuilding, capturing nearly three-quarters of new orders over the past year as the industry’s order book approaches record levels, according to new analysis from BIMCO. The global shipyard order book reached an estimated 203.2 million compensated gross tonnage (CGT) as of September 1, 2026, up 13% from 180 million CGT a year earlier. While slightly below the all-time high of 210.4 million CGT reached in May, the backlog remains above the previous record of 195.4 million CGT set in 2008. Chinese shipyards have been the biggest beneficiaries of the ordering boom, securing 74% of all CGT contracted over the past 12 months. China now controls 64% of the global order book, well ahead of South Korea at 19% and Japan at just 6%. China’s lead is even more pronounced across the major commercial shipping sectors. Its yards hold more than 72% of the order book in each of the six main vessel categories, including containerships, tankers, gas carriers, bulk carriers, other dry cargo ships and RoRo vessels. Together, those segments account for 88% of the global order book. Containerships are driving much of the growth. “Container ships dominate both the order book and its growth over the past 12 months. They account for 30% of CGT on order and 68% of the increase during the past year,” said Niels Rasmussen, BIMCO’s Chief Shipping Analyst. Chinese yards hold an especially commanding 81% share of the global containership order book. But the massive backlog also presents a growing challenge for shipbuilders, particularly in China, where scheduled deliveries are set to far exceed recent production levels. Based on each country’s highest annual output between 2021 and 2025, Chinese shipyards have enough orders to keep them busy for an average of 4.2 years. That compares with just 1.9 years for South Korean yards and 1.7 years for Japanese yards. The challenge is the sheer volume of ships scheduled for delivery. Combined output from China, South Korea and Japan reached 40.1 million CGT in 2025, but scheduled deliveries climb to 55.9 million CGT in 2027 and 60 million CGT in 2028. China faces the steepest increase, with its shipyards scheduled to deliver a record 44 million CGT in 2028, nearly double the 22.7 million CGT delivered in 2025. Meeting those commitments will require a significant increase in production capacity. BIMCO estimates that if capacity is instead measured against the highest annual output delivered or scheduled between 2021 and 2030, China’s order book coverage falls to 2.1 years, compared with 1.6 years for both South Korea and Japan. The figures highlight a potential downside to China’s rapid shipbuilding expansion. While its yards currently enjoy an enormous backlog, the investments needed to meet delivery commitments could leave the industry with excess capacity if demand for new ships slows. “China has further strengthened its position as the world’s leading shipbuilding nation, but its shipyards must raise annual output to new record highs in order to deliver,” Rasmussen said. “The capacity expansion needed to achieve this could increase the risk of underutilisation if contracting weakens in the future.” Sign up for gCaptain’s newsletter and never miss an update Essential maritime and offshore news, insights, and updates delivered daily straight to your inbox Dive into a sea of curated content with our weekly ‘Dispatch’ email.
