(Source: Rosneft) (Bloomberg) — Along Russia’s remote Arctic coast last month, Igor Sechin stood beside a waiting tanker in the freezing cold with a message for Vladimir Putin: After years of construction, the country’s next great oil frontier was finally coming to life. Hundreds of miles of pipeline now connected oil fields to storage tanks and a new port for Vostok Oil, part of an almost $50 billion investment. With Putin watching by video link, Sechin, the powerful head of state-run Rosneft PJSC, asked to begin loading the first tanker with crude. “Permission granted,” Putin said. The ceremony carried particular weight for Russia’s increasingly battered oil industry. Years of war and sanctions are making it harder for oil producers — including Rosneft, the nation’s largest — to maintain volumes today while developing reserves for tomorrow. Rosneft’s Vostok Oil project was supposed to show Russia could still do both. Sechin said it would add as much as 10% to the country’s current output by 2030 and supply millions of barrels to world markets for a century or more. But the milestone obscured a more complicated reality: Years behind schedule, Vostok Oil is still far from becoming Russia’s new oil province. The vast majority of crude flowing through the costly new Arctic network has been diverted from fields that have been producing for years. Just before the terminal opened in September, new oilfields in the Payakha cluster, expected to become key assets of Vostok Oil, accounted for less than 5% of its flows, according to a person familiar with the data, who asked not to be identified to discuss sensitive matters that aren’t public. Satellite imagery shows development continuing, but bringing those fields up to scale will require years more work and investment, according to Bloomberg analysis of the imagery and conversations with analysts. “The development of the company’s fields is carried out in a planned manner, which allows maximum efficiency to be extracted both from existing fields and from new projects,” Rosneft said in a statement, adding that production ramp-ups at Vostok Oil depend on market needs and general economic conditions. Viktor Kurilov, a senior analyst on the oil markets team at Rystad Energy, said building out Vostok Oil “is just one of the challenges Rosneft — and the Russian oil industry — is facing.” Among them is Ukraine’s dramatically expanded campaign of drone strikes against the country’s oil sector, which is inching closer to Vostok Oil facilities and repeatedly damaging refineries run by Rosneft and others in the European part of Russia. One of its biggest, Ryazan, which supplies fuel to Moscow and surrounding regions, has been shut for more than half the time since it was first attacked in May and has run well below full capacity when operating, according to damage assessments seen by Bloomberg. In turn, Rosneft’s finances are suffering. The company’s profits are falling and debt is rising despite what should have been a windfall from the Iran war. Rosneft officials have expressed concern that even a few more months of the war in Ukraine could leave lasting damage across the business, according to people familiar with the matter. The mounting toll to Rosneft and Russia’s wider oil industry helps explain why stopping Ukraine’s strikes on refineries has become such a priority for Moscow. This month, Putin and US President Donald Trump struck a deal opening the door to American purchases of Russian diesel, providing a potential boost as Washington also pressed Kyiv to halt the attacks, an important contributor to the squeeze on global diesel supplies. But an attempted energy truce quickly unraveled, narrowing Rosneft’s avenues for relief — and raising the stakes for a government that gets roughly a fifth of federal revenues from oil and gas. This story is based on conversations with people familiar with the situation at Rosneft, expert analysis and a series of documents reviewed by Bloomberg over the last six months, including damage assessments and company plans for protecting and repairing refineries. Vostok Oil was conceived in a different era, when Russia’s oil refineries were not under constant threat of Ukrainian attacks and production was expected only to grow. Laying out his plans to Putin at a Kremlin meeting in February 2020, Sechin described a vast new Arctic oil province that would create jobs and industry in a remote part of the country. One goal, he said, was to turn the Northern Sea Route into a major global energy corridor. The project was also intended to address a longer-term challenge: Many of Russia’s biggest oilfields had been producing since Soviet times, making new reserves increasingly important to offset their decline. The ambition attracted foreign investors, including commodity trading giant Trafigura, which acquired a 10% stake in 2020, and a Vitol-led consortium, which bought another 5% the following year. Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022 upended those plans. Both Trafigura and the consortium exited, while Western sanctions restricted access to the technology and equipment needed to develop Vostok Oil and build specialized tankers capable of navigating icy waters. As the war dragged on, Ukraine intensified its campaign against Russia’s infrastructure, increasingly targeting the refineries that turn crude oil into fuel. So far this year, Ukrainian drones have carried out at least 114 strikes on Russian refineries, more than double the number over the same period last year, according to a Bloomberg tally, based on public statements from both countries. The attacks have pushed Russian refinery runs to multi-year lows, triggered fuel shortages and forced Moscow to restrict exports of gasoline, diesel and jet fuel. Rosneft has borne a significant share of the damage. The company operates 12 refineries accounting for about a third of Russia’s total oil-processing capacity. Of 15 confirmed drone strikes on the country’s oil-processing plants in September, five targeted major Rosneft facilities supplying fuel to European Russia, the largest consuming region, according to Bloomberg’s tally. Rosneft is “taking appropriate measures to ensure the security and operation of our plants,” and will continue to make sure they are protected, the company said in its statement. “Not a single company petrol station has been closed, and consumers receive fuel in full at stable prices,” it said. In March, while reflecting on Rosneft’s 2025 results, Sechin, a longtime Putin ally, said Russia’s oil producers had faced a “perfect storm” of low oil prices, Western sanctions and soaring borrowing costs. Since then, repeated attacks have forced some of Rosneft’s biggest refineries to operate at reduced capacity or shut altogether. Ryazan has been among the hardest hit, repeatedly coming under attack as Rosneft has sought to restore operations. Another refinery, Syzran, has spent much of the past six months either completely shut or operating at less than a third of capacity, according to data reviewed by Bloomberg, and the company’s Tuapse refinery on the Black Sea coast has been offline since April. Rosneft has managed to restart some refineries within weeks of an attack, only to see them struck again as repairs are completed or nearing completion. The need to repeatedly repair damaged equipment is straining operations and causing costs to pile up to levels that Rosneft officials have privately warned cannot be sustained long-term, according to people familiar with the matter, who asked not to be named to discuss sensitive information. Some plants have deliberately slowed repairs as a result, stretching work that should take days into weeks, the people said. Efforts to protect the facilities with shipping containers, nets and steel cables have proved ineffective against swarms of drones, according to company plans reviewed by Bloomberg. The damage is particularly difficult to repair when strikes hit complex secondary units such as catalytic crackers, reformers and hydrocrackers, whose parts would previously have been sourced from the West. Sanctions are compounding the problems by restricting access to replacement equipment, forcing Rosneft to rely on Russian-made copies and Chinese imports that can take months to obtain and are not always compatible with existing machinery, people familiar with the matter said. More broadly, the International Energy Agency said drone strikes on Russian refineries are having a “cumulative negative effect.” In September, the agency cut its outlook for Russian oil processing over the next 18 months to around 4 million barrels a day, roughly 30% below prewar levels. The financial toll is mounting. Rosneft’s first-half net income fell by almost a fifth to 200 billion rubles ($2.4 billion). Its ratio of net debt to earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization rose to 1.8 times at the end of June, the highest in more than five years, according to quarterly statements dating back to 2020, though three reports over the period don’t disclose the ratio, making estimations of the exact size and scope more challenging. To be sure, conditions have improved since then. Middle East disruptions have pushed the price of Russia’s Urals crude used for tax calculations above $90 a barrel, more than double its level at the start of the year, while Moscow is providing billions of rubles in subsidies to domestic fuel producers, including Rosneft, in recent months. Russia’s central bank has also cut its key rate from a record 21% to 14% over the past two years, though Rosneft has complained that the pace of reductions is “clearly insufficient.” The company’s financial picture and the extent of damage to its infrastructure are being closely monitored by the Qatar Investment Authority, which owns 18.46% of Rosneft and has seen its dividend payments fall sharply during the Ukraine war, according to three Qatari officials familiar with the matter, who asked not to be named to discuss sensitive information. QIA hopes for a swift end to the conflict so its investment is protected longer-term, one of the people said. QIA declined to comment. Rosneft’s problems have coincided with signs of distress at Credit Bank of Moscow PJSC, which market participants and officials view as being in the orbit of Sechin and his oil giant. MKB, as it is known, is dealing with $8 billion in problem loans, Bloomberg reported last month. That development highlights how both Russia’s energy and banking sectors are coming under strain at the same time, a dynamic that Russian finance officials have expressed concern about, people familiar with the matter said. Rosneft said in its statement that its “relations with MKB, as with other Russian banks, are standard,” adding that “neither Rosneft nor its Chief Executive Officer are or have ever been beneficiaries of MKB.” Rosneft faces another financial challenge: the enormous spending still required at Vostok Oil. The project remains heavily dependent on production from Vankor, a group of established fields that began pumping crude in 2009. Its new Arctic terminal gives Rosneft another route to market for that oil, but does little on its own to increase Russia’s output. Rystad Energy, which has analyzed satellite imagery of construction at the project, expects Vostok Oil to produce about 310,000 barrels a day in 2027, with around 90% coming from the Vankor cluster, where fields have been producing for years. Output could rise to 440,000 barrels a day by 2030 — well short of the roughly 1 million Sechin has promised — with the new Payakha fields contributing only about 80,000 barrels a day, according to the consultancy. Getting the oil to market is another obstacle. Rosneft needs specialized tankers to navigate frigid Arctic waters, but Western sanctions have complicated efforts to build them. At least 30 would be needed by 2030 to transport Vostok Oil’s planned output, according to Sergey Vakulenko, an industry veteran and scholar at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace. “They simply don’t exist today,” he said. With Russia’s war in Ukraine well into its fifth year, Putin has secured a potential reprieve from Washington. In an Oct. 9 phone call with Trump, the Russian president said Russia would partially relax its diesel export ban, releasing thousands of barrels a day into the global market. It’s unclear what, if anything, Russia will receive in return. But in the days since, Ukraine has faced temporary restrictions on its military access to SpaceX satellite technology and US intelligence. For Trump, the immediate concern was closer to home. Diesel prices had surged to near-record levels ahead of November’s congressional elections, squeezed by the war in Iran and disruptions to global fuel supplies. The agreement was intended to help bring prices down, though US officials have acknowledged it is unlikely to have much effect on the international diesel market. Washington also pressed Kyiv to halt refinery strikes that had constrained Russian exports. “Unless President Putin agrees to stop attacks on Ukrainian critical infrastructure, or President Trump agrees to give Ukraine additional offensive and defensive capabilities, Kyiv is unlikely to abide by a unilateral ceasefire,” said Fernando Ferreira, director of geopolitical risk at Rapidan Energy Group. The limits of the arrangement soon became apparent. Neither Russia nor Ukraine confirmed the energy ceasefire Trump subsequently announced, and Kyiv resumed refinery attacks last week after accusing Moscow of continuing strikes on its energy infrastructure. Even if the diplomacy eventually produces a more durable pause, Ukraine is already changing the battlefield. In 2022, its attacks reached targets some 650 kilometers (404 miles) from the border. By July this year, drones had struck the Omsk refinery deep in western Siberia, roughly 2,500 kilometers away. Vostok Oil’s Arctic terminal lies another 800 kilometers beyond that, still outside Ukraine’s demonstrated reach. But the vast distances that have long sheltered Russia’s most remote energy assets offer less reassurance than they once did: If the range of Ukrainian drone strikes continues expanding at its recent pace, Vostok Oil could plausibly come within reach within months. At last month’s opening ceremony, Sechin was still looking ahead. Bundled against the cold beside the Valentin Pikul , he told Putin that Vostok Oil would ship 30 million tons of crude as early as the second half of 2027. It was another sign of how much the project has suffered: The terminal was meant to be ready for that volume two years ago. © 2026 Bloomberg L.P. Photo courtesy McAllister Towing The global fleet of dual-fuel containerships and vehicle carriers has surpassed 500 vessels, with shipowners committing more than $200 billion to ships capable of running on alternative fuels, according to new figures from the World Shipping Council (WSC). The latest WSC Dual-Fuel Fleet Dashboard shows 503 dual-fuel vessels in service as of September 2026, a 41% increase from 358 a year earlier. Another 849 ships are on order, bringing the combined total to 1,352 vessels. The figures highlight the scale of investment underway as container lines and vehicle carriers prepare for a transition to lower-emission fuels, even as uncertainty over future environmental regulations continues to cloud the industry’s outlook. “The container ship and vehicle carrier industry have committed more than $200 billion to ships that can run on cleaner fuels, with more than 500 already sailing and hundreds more on the way,” said WSC President and CEO Joe Kramek. “The investment is happening, but these ships need commercially competitive alternative fuels to deliver their full potential to reduce emissions.” Dual-fuel vessels are designed to operate on conventional marine fuels as well as alternative fuels, giving operators flexibility as new fuel supplies and infrastructure develop. However, their ability to reduce emissions depends heavily on the availability and cost of cleaner fuels. According to WSC, alternative-fuel-capable vessels now account for 65% of containerships and 97% of vehicle carriers on order, measured by deadweight tonnage. That compares with just 23% across the rest of the global shipping fleet. Despite that shift, orders for conventionally fueled ships have also increased over the past year as the overall orderbook continues to expand. The mixed picture comes amid continued uncertainty over the International Maritime Organization’s proposed Net-Zero Framework, which would introduce a global marine fuel standard and greenhouse gas pricing mechanism. Adoption of the framework was postponed in October 2025, with negotiations set to resume later this year. WSC argues that a global regulatory framework is needed to close the cost gap between conventional fuels and renewable and near-zero-emission alternatives while giving shipowners and fuel producers the certainty needed to invest. Without an international agreement, the industry also faces the prospect of an increasingly fragmented system of regional emissions rules, adding costs and complexity to global shipping. “Ships ordered today will be operating for decades. Shipping companies and fuel producers need certainty to make the investments that will shape the future fleet and its fuel supply,” Kramek said. The IMO is scheduled to hold its next Marine Environment Protection Committee meeting from November 30 to December 3, with a possible resumed session on the Net-Zero Framework on December 4. “We trust IMO member states can come together to deliver that framework,” Kramek said. “Every delay means increased uncertainty, making the transition harder and costlier for the global economy.” Sign up for gCaptain’s newsletter and never miss an update Essential maritime and offshore news, insights, and updates delivered daily straight to your inbox Dive into a sea of curated content with our weekly ‘Dispatch’ email. REUTERS/Ints Kalnins ATHENS, Oct 22 (Reuters) – The Greek finance ministry said on Thursday it was implementing sanctions in place linked to Iran and that it backed efforts to effectively combat money laundering and the financing of terrorism. The statement comes after the US Treasury Department said on Wednesday it imposed sanctions on Karnakis & Karnakis , a law firm based in Greece and Panama, saying it had for years provided legal assistance to Iranian shipping networks. The Treasury also said that the US Financial Crimes Enforcement Network issued an administrative subpoena to advance an investigation into a Greek bank, which it did not name. The Greek finance ministry said it had taken note of the US Treasury statement, adding that “all available information is being evaluated, and appropriate measures are being taken in accordance with established procedures and applicable national, EU, and international law.” (Reporting by Angeliki Koutantou; Editing by Aidan Lewis) (c) Copyright Thomson Reuters 2026. articles.title: ID Logistics revenue jumps 25.6% in Q3 as North America drives growth
articles.summary: ID Logistics reported a 25.6% increase in revenue during the third quarter of 2026, supported by strong growth in North America and continued expansion across its international operations. The contract logistics group generated revenue of €1.18 billion, compared with €937.8 million in the same period last year....
articles.body: ID Logistics reported a 25.6% increase in revenue during the third quarter of 2026, supported by strong growth in North America and continued expansion across its international operations. The contract logistics group generated revenue of €1.18 billion, compared with €937.8 million in the same period last year. Like-for-like growth reached 25%, accelerating from 22.6% in the second quarter and 17.2% in the first quarter. For the first nine months of 2026, revenue increased by 20.9% to €3.26 billion, while like-for-like growth stood at 21.7%. The company launched 10 new operations during the third quarter, bringing the total to 27 since the beginning of the year. North America leads regional growth North America recorded the strongest regional performance, with like-for-like revenue growth of 48.1% in the third quarter. Revenue in the region reached €265.9 million. Europe excluding France generated €543.9 million in revenue, representing like-for-like growth of 23.4%. In France, revenue reached €272.3 million, up 8.3% on a like-for-like basis. Other regions reported revenue of €95.8 million, with like-for-like growth of 35.9%, partly supported by the launch of operations in Australia. Nearly 80% of ID Logistics’ business is now generated outside France. New logistics operations support expansion The company continued expanding its contract logistics network during the quarter. In the United States, ID Logistics secured a third operation for Nutrabolt, a sports nutrition and energy drinks company. The operation will be based at a dedicated 60,000-square-meter facility in Jacksonville, Florida. In Canada, the group plans to open its third site before the end of 2026. The mechanized facility, located in Eastern Canada, will handle apparel and footwear for an existing customer described as a global e-commerce leader. The Canadian site will represent ID Logistics’ first fashion logistics operation in North America. “Our business model is scaling up,” said Eric Hémar, Chairman and CEO of ID Logistics. Hémar highlighted the group’s expanding international presence, investments in technology and continued growth in new operations. Looking ahead, ID Logistics expects another year of strong growth in 2026. Its immediate priorities include increasing activity at recently opened facilities, implementing new customer projects and preparing for peak demand during Black Friday and the holiday season. The company is scheduled to publish its fourth-quarter revenue figures on January 26, 2027.

REUTERS/Antranik Tavitian Iran’s Revolutionary Guards claimed Thursday that seven commercial vessels were struck overnight in the Persian Gulf and Strait of Hormuz, including four ships conducting oil transfers, prompting President Donald Trump to accuse Tehran of fabricating attacks to drive up oil prices ahead of the U.S. midterm elections. The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Navy said four vessels conducting ship-to-ship oil transfers in the northern Persian Gulf were struck simultaneously on Wednesday and caught fire. The vessels were allegedly transferring oil for an American company using routes Iran considers illegal. In a separate claim, the IRGC said three additional vessels struck naval mines west of the Strait of Hormuz, causing fires that left them disabled, according to Reuters . None of the seven incidents has been independently confirmed. Iran did not identify the ships, their owners or the American company allegedly involved. There were also no immediate details about casualties or potential oil spills. UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO), which tracks attacks on commercial shipping in the region, has not issued new incident reports corresponding to the claims. President Trump responded Thursday by accusing Iran of inventing attacks as part of an effort to influence oil prices ahead of the November 3 elections. “Iran is doing everything they can to drive up the price of Oil prior to the U.S. Midterm Election,” Trump wrote on Truth Social. “They are even making up fake hits, mines, and everything else, because more Oil is coming through the Hormuz Strait now than it did even prior to the beginning of the Conflict.” The president’s accusation follows weeks of increasingly aggressive Iranian statements claiming that merchant vessels using routes outside Tehran’s control have been struck by mines or other weapons. But the absence of UKMTO reports does not necessarily mean the attacks did not occur. In its October 16 weekly assessment , UKMTO acknowledged that it was struggling to establish the true number of attacks because the majority of vessels targeted were not reporting incidents directly to the organization. UKMTO said it was aware of additional attacks through other sources but could not publish warnings without sufficient verification. That reporting gap has become increasingly important as the United States and Iran offer competing accounts of what is happening in the waterway. The most significant element of Iran’s latest announcement is its claim to have targeted four vessels actively engaged in ship-to-ship oil transfers. If confirmed, the attacks would appear to mark the first reported direct targeting of an active ship-to-ship oil transfer operation during the conflict. Such transfers have become a critical part of the improvised shipping network that has allowed Persian Gulf producers to restore much of their oil exports despite repeated attacks in the Strait of Hormuz. Under a system operating with U.S. military assistance, tankers make short voyages through the strait, frequently with their AIS transponders switched off, before transferring cargoes to other vessels waiting in the Gulf of Oman. The receiving tankers then carry the oil to international markets. The system has allowed producers to move substantial volumes of crude without relying on routes controlled by Iran, although at extraordinary cost. The International Energy Agency reported Wednesday that tanker freight costs from the Middle East Gulf to Asia had climbed above $37 per barrel, more than five times prewar levels. For a fully loaded 2-million-barrel VLCC, that translates to more than $74 million in freight costs alone. The location of Iran’s latest alleged attacks, in the northern Persian Gulf, is distinct from the Gulf of Oman transfer operations used by the U.S.-facilitated shuttle system. There is currently no independent evidence connecting the four vessels to that network. Nevertheless, a confirmed attack on vessels during cargo transfers would represent a potentially significant expansion of the threat to regional oil shipping. Iran’s latest claims also follow a series of announcements alleging that tankers have struck naval mines while attempting to transit the Strait of Hormuz without Iranian authorization. Those claims have repeatedly been challenged by maritime security authorities. In its October 18 advisory , the Joint Maritime Information Center (JMIC) addressed Iranian statements that two supertankers had struck mines the previous day, saying there was “no substantiation to these claims.” U.S. Central Command has also rejected previous Iranian mine-strike announcements as false, accusing the IRGC of attempting to intimidate commercial shipping through disinformation. However, JMIC continues to warn of a credible threat of renewed mining in and around the strait’s traffic separation scheme. Its latest assessment maintains the threat level for the Strait of Hormuz at SEVERE, with further deliberate attacks considered highly likely. Trump’s assertion that more oil is moving through Hormuz than before the conflict also comes amid conflicting assessments of the recovery in Gulf exports. Overall Middle East oil shipments have approached or exceeded prewar levels in recent weeks, aided by an expanded network of pipelines, short-haul tanker voyages and offshore transfers. But the recovery in total exports does not necessarily mean that more oil is moving through the strait itself. According to reporting by The Wall Street Journal cited by gCaptain , flows through Hormuz, including offshore transfers, remained at approximately 82% of prewar levels, even as overall regional exports recovered. UKMTO’s latest weekly overview also recorded just 254 vessel transits during the seven days ending October 14, approximately 70% below pre-conflict levels. Those figures include U.S.-reported facilitated transits that UKMTO says it cannot independently verify. The figures measure different things—vessel movements, oil flows through Hormuz and overall regional exports—but illustrate the difficulty of determining how much shipping has actually recovered. Meanwhile, the security situation continues to deteriorate. UKMTO documented 12 attacks during the reporting period ending October 16, including 10 in the Strait of Hormuz. One vessel was lost, two were disabled or left not under command, and the outcomes of three others remained uncertain. articles.summary: Windward intelligence report highlights tanker and tug attacks, threats to subsea cables, an emerging oil spill and a sanctioned Russian tanker testing U.S. naval restrictions.Maritime security risks across the Strait of Hormuz, Arabian Gulf…

Windward intelligence report highlights tanker and tug attacks, threats to subsea cables, an emerging oil spill and a sanctioned Russian tanker testing U.S. naval restrictions. Maritime security risks across the Strait of Hormuz, Arabian Gulf and Gulf of Oman are expanding beyond attacks on commercial tankers, with threats now extending to subsea communications infrastructure, offshore support vessels and coastal facilities. An October 22 intelligence report from Windward Maritime identifies five developments that illustrate the widening scope of the conflict and its implications for commercial shipping, energy transportation and regional infrastructure. Iran Threatens Subsea Communications Cables Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) has identified subsea internet cables crossing the Strait of Hormuz as potential targets. On October 19, IRGC spokesman Hossein Mohebbi warned that new targets and weapons would be unveiled, citing seven major communications cables beneath the strait. Windward identifies six operational cable systems crossing Hormuz, with additional systems scheduled for 2027. Iraq, Kuwait, Bahrain and Qatar are particularly vulnerable because their subsea communications routes to markets outside the Gulf pass through the strait. For Iraq, the vulnerability is compounded by all three operational cables landing at Al Faw. Disruptions could affect regional communications infrastructure well beyond commercial shipping. However, Windward notes that two cable systems also connect to Iran, meaning attacks could damage Iranian connectivity. Live subsea cable landings per country across the Arabian Gulf, Strait of Hormuz and Gulf of Oman, with countries ranked by exposure. Source: Windward Maritime AITM Platform. Small-Boat Attack Signals Changing Tactics On October 16, a Liberia-flagged Suezmax tanker was likely struck by a rocket-propelled grenade fired from a small boat approximately 78 nautical miles northeast of Al Jubail, Saudi Arabia. According to a UK Maritime Trade Operations advisory cited by Windward, the attack damaged the tanker's aft port quarter, although no casualties were reported. The vessel continued sailing, reportedly carrying approximately 1.09 million barrels of Saudi and UAE crude bound for Kuwait. Earlier that day, another tanker was struck by an unidentified projectile nearby, prompting the safe evacuation of its crew. Windward considers the suspected small-boat attack significant because previous incidents predominantly involved drones or projectiles concentrated around Hormuz. The development suggests threats to shipping are extending deeper into the Gulf, potentially affecting war-risk assessments for regional port calls. Tug Attack Threatens Gulf Oil Transfer Operations A Netherlands-flagged tug, identified by TradeWinds as JIF Barracuda, was reportedly struck by two unidentified projectiles northeast of Khor Fakkan, UAE, on October 18. One crew member suffered minor injuries, but the tug continued its voyage. UKMTO did not attribute responsibility for the attack. Windward identifies the incident as the second tug strike since the conflict began and the 27th maritime attack recorded during October. The location is significant. Khor Fakkan, Fujairah and Sohar support extensive ship-to-ship crude oil transfers outside Hormuz. Windward estimates that these anchorages handled approximately 3.97 million barrels per day in transfers during October 12–14, representing roughly half the crude shipped from the Gulf of Oman during that period. Attacks on tugs threaten the support infrastructure needed to maintain tanker movements, cargo transfers and salvage operations. Tanker Oil Leak Threatens UAE Coastline Satellite imagery collected October 19 identified a VLCC-size tanker apparently leaking oil approximately 25 kilometers north of Umm Al Quwain. Windward observed a slick extending approximately 1.5 km behind the vessel. Its drift modeling projected possible shoreline contamination beginning October 22, with oil potentially approaching Hamriyah Port, Ajman Port, coastal mangroves and desalination infrastructure through October 24. The company cautions that its projections do not account for cleanup operations or the leak being stopped. Sanctioned Russian Tanker Tests U.S. Naval Line A Russian-flagged oil and chemical tanker approached and crossed a U.S. Navy restriction line inbound to the Gulf of Oman on October 18. According to Windward, the vessel slowed from nine knots to approximately one knot, loitered and subsequently reversed course toward the Arabian Sea on October 19. The EU- and UK-sanctioned tanker was assessed as potentially carrying approximately 65,400 barrels of naphtha. Windward describes the movement as an apparent test of the naval restriction line, although the vessel's intended destination remains unknown. Taken together, the five developments point to an increasingly complex operating environment for shipowners, charterers and marine service providers. Beyond the direct threat to vessels, the conflict is exposing vulnerabilities in the infrastructure that supports regional trade, energy exports and maritime operations.

REUTERS/Stringer/File Photo QatarEnergy has signed two long-term agreements to purchase up to 4 million tonnes of U.S. liquefied natural gas annually from Cheniere Energy through 2054, as the Gulf producer continues to grapple with damage to its own export facilities from the war with Iran. The agreements, announced Thursday, cover 2 million tonnes per annum (MTPA) each from Cheniere’s Sabine Pass facility in Louisiana and Corpus Christi facility in Texas. Deliveries are expected to begin in 2031 and continue through 2054. Under the contracts, QatarEnergy will purchase the LNG on a free-on-board (FOB) basis, taking responsibility for transporting cargoes from the U.S. terminals. Pricing will be linked to the Henry Hub natural gas benchmark plus a fixed fee. The deal comes as QatarEnergy faces significant disruptions to its own LNG production following Iranian missile strikes on its Ras Laffan Industrial City in March. The attacks damaged two LNG production trains with a combined capacity of 12.8 MTPA, knocking out approximately 17% of Qatar’s export capacity. QatarEnergy has warned that repairs could take three to five years, potentially costing $20 billion annually in lost revenue and disrupting long-term supply commitments to customers in Europe and Asia. While the U.S. contracts will not begin delivering cargoes until the early 2030s, they will give QatarEnergy an additional source of supply outside the Persian Gulf, where energy infrastructure and shipping have faced mounting threats during the conflict. QatarEnergy described the agreements as part of its broader strategy to diversify its global LNG portfolio. “This major long-term purchase will expand and diversify our global LNG portfolio and advance our ability to meet the evolving requirements of the market,” said Saad Sherida Al-Kaabi, Qatar’s minister of state for energy affairs and CEO of QatarEnergy. For Cheniere, the agreements secure another major long-term customer for its U.S. Gulf Coast operations. The company currently operates approximately 56 MTPA of LNG production capacity across Sabine Pass and Corpus Christi, with another 5 MTPA under construction. One million tonnes annually under the new Sabine Pass agreement remains contingent on a final investment decision for the first phase of the terminal’s planned expansion. The deal highlights QatarEnergy’s growing role not only as a major LNG producer but also as an international LNG trader, while adding another long-term source of U.S. Gulf Coast cargoes that can reach global markets without passing through the Strait of Hormuz. articles.body: Asia Offshore Renewables Marco Polo Marine expands Korean offshore push with new JV Adis Ajdin October 22, 2026 0 448 1 minute read Marco Polo Marine Marco Polo Marine Singapore-listed offshore vessel owner and shipyard group Marco Polo Marine has established a joint venture in South Korea with local partner NSEL, strengthening its presence in the country’s offshore vessel market. The new company, Baramgil Offshore, will focus on vessel operations, management and chartering, with NSEL holding a 51% stake and Baramgil Corporation taking the remaining 49%. Baramgil Corporation is 90% owned by Marco Polo Marine’s Taiwan-based affiliate PKR Offshore, in which the Singapore group holds an indirect 49% interest. The venture has been established with an initial paid-up capital of about $107,000, with Marco Polo Marine funding its investment through internal resources. The company said the move would have no material impact on its earnings or net tangible assets for the financial year ending September 2027. The latest move builds on an existing partnership between PKR Offshore and NSEL, established in 2023 to pursue opportunities in South Korea’s offshore wind sector. The partners made their first move into the Korean market in 2024, deploying a Korean-flagged crew transfer vessel (CTV) for offshore wind work. The MP Corus was among the vessels brought into the market to support wind farm construction activities off the country’s southwest coast. Marco Polo Marine has also been expanding its offshore wind support fleet across Asia. In July, the company secured a multi-year framework agreement with Siemens Gamesa covering two commissioning service operation vessels (CSOVs), primarily for projects in Taiwan, with potential deployments in South Korea and Japan. The agreement is scheduled to begin in 2029, with provisions for an earlier start in 2028. articles.summary: Miros, a Norwegian specialist in radar-based real-time ocean surface measurement, has introduced a 3D vessel view providing crews and operators with a consolidated view of the accurately measured sea state surrounding their vessel. The new 3D interface in WaveSystem…
articles.body: Miros Launches 3D Vessel View For Sea-State Monitoring Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 22, 2026 © Miros Miros, a Norwegian specialist in radar-based real-time ocean surface measurement, has introduced a 3D vessel view providing crews and operators with a consolidated view of the accurately measured sea state surrounding their vessel. The new 3D interface in WaveSystem, a wave monitoring system for weather-critical offshore vessel operations, shows where each wave measurement is taken. It brings each installed measurement source, its measurement area and the key wave values together in one intuitive display, providing a bird’s-eye view of the sea state data most relevant to safeguard operations. The feature is included for WaveSystem subscribers worldwide at no additional cost. Wave conditions can differ around a vessel due to wave direction, vessel heading, hull geometry, shielding, and measurement location. Where multiple measurement sources are installed, comparing readings can help teams clearly understand differences between measurement areas and sea conditions affecting specific working areas. Bridge and deck crew can easily assess conditions port and starboard, check the waves at a specific working area such as a gangway or ROV launch point, and spot differences between measurement areas before they affect the operation, turning a weather-critical operation into a controlled one. The visualization shows measurement sources, areas, and values in relation to the vessel. It does not represent a reconstructed 3D sea surface.

articles.title: Cook Inlet LNG steps up Alaska energy push with TDI-Brooks survey
articles.summary: TDI-Brooks has completed a geotechnical mission, bolstering Cook Inlet LNG’s efforts to shore up Southcentral Alaska’s energy supplies.
articles.body: Vessels October 22, 2026 · 15 hours ago Cook Inlet LNG steps up Alaska energy push with TDI-Brooks survey TDI-Brooks has completed a geotechnical mission, bolstering Cook Inlet LNG’s efforts to shore up Southcentral Alaska’s energy supplies. MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email N5K on back of RV Poseidon with the rig working close to it in the background Credit: Ivan Svrcek/TDI-Brooks U.S.-headquartered geotechnical and offshore survey research and service company TDI-Brooks has wrapped up a critical geotechnical campaign for Cook Inlet LNG, a strategic initiative designed to secure natural gas supplies for Southcentral Alaska, delivering vital subsurface data to support the project's anchor selection and helping bring the developer’s floating import terminal aspirations closer to reality. TDI-Brooks has concluded a geotechnical project for the Cook Inlet LNG project (CI LNG) in Cook Inlet, Alaska, providing its Neptune N5K cone penetration testing (CPT) system for an anchor site characterization study. The work supported the project developer by collecting subsurface soil data to inform anchor selection. According to the U.S. player, the study covered different locations within the project site with a scope of 16 CPTs in water depths ranging from 10 to 25 meters. Operations were conducted from the R/V Poseidon , a third-party vessel working in the region, demonstrating the firm’s ability to deploy specialized geotechnical equipment aboard locally available vessels. The Neptune N5K is part of the company’s range of portable toolkits available for deployment worldwide, which allow clients to pair regional vessel resources with TDI-Brooks’ equipment and technical expertise, providing flexible support for offshore site investigations and infrastructure projects. The Cook Inlet LNG project is an energy security initiative designed to address declining natural gas reserves in the Cook Inlet basin of Southcentral Alaska to stave off a potential energy shortfall for heating and electricity by serving as a near-term bridge solution to import gas. The project is designed to use a floating storage and regasification unit (FSRU) anchored offshore east of West Foreland, near the existing Osprey production platform, utilizing existing subsea pipelines to minimize environmental and construction footprints. TDI-Brooks’ geotechnical study was done to test the seafloor soil properties to figure out how to safely anchor the FSRU and its infrastructure in Cook Inlet's harsh marine environment. The completion of this study comes months after the U.S. firm was hired by Delfin LNG to provide offshore geophysical and geotechnical survey services for the Delfin deepwater port project offshore Louisiana. Nexans will conduct engineering activities for a comprehensive cable system incorporating both subsea and land cable infrastructure, building on its longstanding experience delivering complex interconnection projects and its established presence in the region. The project will leverage the company’s expertise across engineering, manufacturing, and installation, with particular attention to be given to environmental stewardship throughout project planning and execution, reflecting the ecological sensitivity of the project area. articles.summary: "On 1 September 2026, the global shipyard order book reached an estimated 203.2m Compensated Gross Tonnage (CGT), up 13% from 180.0m CGT a year earlier,” says Niels Rasmussen, Chief Shipping Analyst at BIMCO.This is slightly below the all-time…
articles.body: Global Shipyard Orderbook Up 13%, China Dominates Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 22, 2026 "On 1 September 2026, the global shipyard order book reached an estimated 203.2m Compensated Gross Tonnage (CGT), up 13% from 180.0m CGT a year earlier,” says Niels Rasmussen, Chief Shipping Analyst at BIMCO. This is slightly below the all-time high of 210.4m CGT reached in May but remains above the previous record of 195.4m CGT from 2008. Much of the growth has been captured by Chinese shipyards, who secured 74% of the CGT contracted during the past year. This has further strengthened China’s position as the world’s largest shipbuilding nation. Chinese shipyards now hold 64% of the global order book while South Korean shipyards hold 19% and Japanese 6%. China’s dominance extends across the major cargo-carrying ship sectors. Its shipyards hold more than 72% of the order book in each of the six main sectors: container, tanker, gas tanker, dry bulk, other dry cargo and RoRo. Combined, these sectors account for 88% of the global order book. Their yards’ largest share is in the container ship segment, with 81% of the order book. “Container ships dominate both the order book and its growth over the past 12 months. They account for 30% of CGT on order and 68% of the increase during the past year,” says Rasmussen. Additionally, Chinese shipyards currently have better capacity coverage than their South Korean and Japanese competitors. If each shipyard’s current capacity is assumed to equal its highest annual CGT output during 2021–2025, Chinese shipyards hold orders equivalent to an average of 4.2 years of capacity. The corresponding figures for South Korean and Japanese yards are 1.9 and 1.7 years. Combined deliveries from China, South Korea and Japan peaked at 40.1m CGT in 2025, but 55.9m CGT and 60.0m CGT are currently scheduled for delivery in 2027 and 2028. Chinese yards, in particular, will have to raise output to manage the scheduled deliveries. Current capacity could therefore be assumed to equal the highest annual CGT delivered or scheduled for delivery during 2021–2030. In that case, average coverage falls to 2.1 years for Chinese shipyards and 1.6 years for both South Korean and Japanese shipyards. “China has further strengthened its position as the world’s leading shipbuilding nation, but its shipyards must raise annual output to new record highs in order to deliver. Chinese yards are scheduled to deliver a record 44.0m CGT in 2028, nearly twice the 22.7m CGT delivered in 2025. The capacity expansion needed to achieve this could increase the risk of underutilisation if contracting weakens in the future,” says Rasmussen.

articles.summary: Idan Ofer’s Eastern Pacific Shipping (EPS) has named its first ammonia dual-fuel very large ammonia carrier (VLAC) at HD Hyundai Heavy Industries in South Korea, bringing the 93,000 cu m vessel closer to its commercial debut. The Singapore-based owner christened the vessel Terra Clove at the Ulsan yard, with delivery...
articles.body: Asia Gas Eastern Pacific takes wraps off first ammonia dual-fuel VLAC Adis Ajdin October 22, 2026 0 436 1 minute read EPS / MMMCZCS EPS / MMMCZCS Idan Ofer’s Eastern Pacific Shipping (EPS) has named its first ammonia dual-fuel very large ammonia carrier (VLAC) at HD Hyundai Heavy Industries in South Korea, bringing the 93,000 cu m vessel closer to its commercial debut. The Singapore-based owner christened the vessel Terra Clove at the Ulsan yard, with delivery scheduled for November following sea trials. The newbuilding is the first ammonia dual-fuel commercial vessel to be registered under the Singapore flag and the first of two such ships being built by HD Hyundai for EPS. Designed to transport ammonia as cargo and burn it as propulsion fuel, the 230 m long vessel is fitted with Everllence’s 6G60ME-LGIA two-stroke engine, which completed factory acceptance testing in April and passed type approval testing in June. The ship features four cargo tanks and dedicated ammonia fuel handling and safety systems, including leak detection and emissions management equipment. The project dates back to June 2022, when EPS joined forces with the Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore (MPA), HD Hyundai Heavy Industries and classification society ABS to develop an ammonia-powered gas carrier. The partners have since worked on the vessel’s design, safety requirements and regulatory approval, with particular attention to ammonia handling, ventilation, emissions and crew preparedness. The milestone also coincided with EPS signing a strategic partnership with the Mærsk Mc-Kinney Møller Center for Zero Carbon Shipping during the naming ceremony. The two will collaborate on alternative fuels, dual-fuel propulsion, energy efficiency and ammonia safety, including research into methane and ammonia emissions. A joint white paper covering VLAC design, operational safety and crew training is expected later this year. The development adds to EPS’s expanding position in the ammonia carrier market. Earlier this year, the company returned to China’s Jiangnan Shipyard for two additional 90,000 cu m VLACs, scheduled for delivery in the first half of 2028. Those vessels will feature LPG dual-fuel propulsion, rather than engines designed to burn ammonia. The latest contract followed a series of six 93,000 cu m VLACs previously booked at Jiangnan, as EPS continued building up its gas carrier fleet alongside investments in alternative propulsion technologies. articles.body: Americas Europe Offshore Viridien sharpens exploration picture beyond Guyana’s Stabroek block Bojan Lepic October 22, 2026 0 233 1 minute read Viridien Viridien French geophysical company Viridien has launched the first phase of a major seismic reimaging programme offshore Guyana, targeting more than 10,000 sq km of existing 3D data in and around the country’s emerging shallow-water exploration acreage. The project covers the Kaieteur, Georgetown, Kanuku, and Corentyne legacy surveys and is intended to sharpen subsurface imaging updip of the prolific ExxonMobil-operated Stabroek block. Viridien said it would combine the reprocessed information with newly acquired 3D seismic to create a continuous regional dataset exceeding 14,000 sq km. Preliminary results are expected in the first quarter of 2027. The company, formerly known as CGG, holds exclusive access and commercialisation rights to the legacy datasets. It said the programme had attracted strong industry backing but did not disclose the value of the work or identify participating customers. The work comes against the backdrop of Guyana’s broader effort to expand exploration beyond Stabroek, where successive discoveries have transformed the country’s offshore oil sector. In March, Guyana’s natural resources ministry announced a wider multi-client 3D acquisition and imaging initiative with Viridien and Chinese geophysical company BGP, covering roughly 25,000 sq km of shallow-water acreage. The programme covers 11 blocks from the country’s 2022 licensing round. BGP will acquire new seismic data, while Viridien will provide imaging using techniques including time-lag full-waveform inversion. articles.body: Bunkering Europe Gas Tankers Maersk Tankers lines up EU backing for four VLAC ammonia conversions Adis Ajdin October 22, 2026 0 499 1 minute read Maersk Tankers Maersk Tankers Danish shipowner Maersk Tankers has moved closer to converting four very large ammonia carriers to run on the cargo they transport after its retrofit proposal was selected for support under the European Union’s Innovation Fund. The project, known as RIPPLE, involves installing dual-fuel, two-stroke ammonia engines on four vessels in the company’s expanding gas carrier fleet. The European Commission has invited the project to begin grant agreement preparations, although the amount of funding has not yet been finalised. Crucially, Maersk Tankers said any decision to proceed would depend on securing commercial commitments from customers. The proposed conversions would allow the vessels to use ammonia as propulsion fuel rather than relying solely on conventional marine fuels. According to the Commission’s project description, RIPPLE would demonstrate the EU’s first dual-fuel ammonia retrofit on a VLAC. The project is expected to avoid more than 1.2m tonnes of carbon dioxide-equivalent emissions over ten years, assuming the conversions and planned operations go ahead. Maersk Tankers is building up a fleet of ten 93,000 cu m VLACs at South Korea’s HD Hyundai Samho. The company re-entered the gas carrier sector in 2023 with an initial four-ship order, followed by additional option exercises. The vessels were specified with the possibility of converting to ammonia propulsion, although installation of the necessary engines has always depended on commercial and regulatory conditions. The latest funding selection moves that option a step closer to implementation. The Commission selected 77 projects under its latest Innovation Fund round, with final grant agreements expected to be determined during the first quarter of 2027. Join the leading maritime news network By David Brunnstrom WASHINGTON, Oct 22 (Reuters) – The Philippines is exploring deeper cooperation with Taiwan on protecting undersea cables and addressing “gray-zone” activity, despite Manila’s one-China policy, which recognizes Beijing and not Taipei, a Philippine diplomat said on Wednesday. The Philippines and Taiwan have repeatedly complained about Chinese activities designed to pressure the countries without direct confrontation. China claims Taiwan as its own territory and has overlapping claims with both Taiwan and the Philippines in the South China Sea. Felipe F. Carino III, Manila’s deputy chief of mission in Washington, told a seminar this “pragmatic and practical approach” with Taiwan was necessary to protect mutual interests in the Bashi Channel between Taiwan and the Philippines. Speaking to Washington’s Center for a New American Security, Carino linked cable security to South China Sea tensions, but did not mention China by name. He said security of undersea cables was vital given that they carried nearly all intercontinental data flows “and that 60-67% of cyber incidents happen in our region.” “These are very important features that should be protected, so much so that we are exploring deeper cooperation with our friends in Taiwan,” Carino said, adding that the Philippines was doing so “notwithstanding our one China policy.” He said the Philippines and Taiwan were exploring “practical and more pragmatic approaches in cooperation, including knowledge-sharing and capacity building” and added: “We see this cooperation leading towards … addressing the gray-zone issues in our part of the world.” China warned the Philippines that it should “strictly adhere to the one-China Principle with real actions” and sent Taiwan a similar message, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said on Thursday. Asked if this cooperation could include joint patrols or accountability for vessels that disrupt communications, Carino said he did not have details, but said: “I’m sure that this is a constantly evolving cooperation, and some of the things that you mentioned may be actually coming to fruition.” Taipei has stepped up efforts to protect undersea communications links, which are vital to the island’s connections to the rest of the world, after several incidents involving cables and China-linked vessels. This month, the Philippines’ coast guard said it had deployed its largest vessel and an aircraft to challenge a Chinese research ship operating off northern Batanes province near undersea cable corridors . At the same seminar, Andrea Yang, Taiwan’s deputy representative in Washington, referred to the jailing in Taiwan of a Chinese ship captain over damage to an undersea cable. She said Taiwan would put more resources into developing unmanned systems to improve maritime surveillance. Yang said interference with undersea cables was an issue that should be taken up by the United Nations, which should consider mechanisms to prevent “bad behavior.” (Reporting by David Brunnstrom; Additional reporting by Eduardo Baptista in Beijing; Editing by Don Durfee, David Gregorio and Xevi Fontdegloria) (c) Copyright Thomson Reuters 2026.
